and a procedural marker (instructs a construction):

| | sentences | share |
|---|---|---|
| carry **both** marker kinds | 157 | **57.9%** |
| procedural only | 68 | 25.1% |
| declarative only | 43 | 15.9% |
| neither | 3 | 1.1% |

The bar is the one R32 prediction 2 already registered for a sibling question — **fewer than half** —
and 57.9% is over it. The failure is not a threshold artefact: a first, looser marker set that also
counted `when`, `which` and `so` as declarative put the same share at **65.7%**. A verdict that
survives a change of markers is a verdict; this one does.

The reason is in the sentences themselves. *"A query that joins a one-to-many table and filters on
an aggregate of the many side must deduplicate the projected entity column, because each matching
child row otherwise produces a duplicate parent row"* states a consequence and gives a construction
in one breath, and that is the normal shape here rather than an outlier.

**What the leftovers show, reported as leftovers.** The 111 pure-form sentences still classify 817
questions, 100 of them mixed, 617 of them with no pure rule at all. On what remains:

| group | n | Δ vs no memory |
|---|---|---|
| packs whose pure rules are procedural | 487 | **+1.64pp** |
| packs whose pure rules are declarative | 330 | **−2.12pp** |
| packs holding both | 100 | +3.00pp |
| packs with no pure rule | 617 | +0.16pp |

The gap is **+3.76pp [0.25, 7.76]**, and it is larger where no ungrounded name was imported —
**+5.15pp [2.44, 7.97]** over the 716 questions in these two groups whose query introduced no name
(1,379 questions introduced none at all; the rest carry no pure rule). **That is the opposite of
what prediction 3 said**: the registration expected the procedural rules to be the damaged ones, on
the reasoning that a pack's names would be the mechanism only if the declarative ones were harmful.
The declarative pack is the harmed one.

**And it does not survive the database.** The gap is positive in 6 of the 11 databases, negative in
4, and exactly zero in one — so 6 of 10 non-zero signs, which a two-sided sign test puts at
**p = 0.754**. The pooled +3.76pp is not a direction the corpus holds: `financial` gives −7.69pp and
`european_football_2` gives +10.38pp, and both are the same classifier applied to the same form in
two databases.
Two readings that disagree this cleanly are the reading that the axis is not usable and the reading
that it is — and the census already decided that, so nothing here is promoted. It is recorded
because the next round's question is why the declarative direction keeps coming back, not whether
this round resolved it.

### The defect: an id names a slot, not a rule

`query-diff.ts` looked a rule up by its `id`, and the id is reused across folds. `k_01hf7uaqrd_550r9`
names four unrelated rules — numeric literals in `california_schools` in fold 0, integer division in
`toxicology` in fold 1, a foreign-key filter in fold 2, `NOT LIKE` status text in fold 3. A `Map`
keyed by id collapses 1,066 rows into 229 keys and answers with whichever fold was read last, so
every per-rule reading in §141 was being taken over **fold 4's sentences** while the questions were
spread over all five.

The lookup is now `fold:id`, and the rule-level read changed:

| | keyed by `id` | keyed by `fold:id` |
|---|---|---|
| rows naming an identifier | 138 (12.95%) | **149 (13.98%)** |
| questions flagged at rule level | 385 (25.1%) | **407 (26.5%)** |
| Δ on flagged | +2.86pp | **+0.49pp** |
| Δ on the rest | −0.52pp | **+0.27pp** |
| precision / recall against F1 | 13.0% / 32.3% | **11.3% / 29.7%** |

**The direction of §141's conclusion is unchanged and its margin was inflated.** Before the fix the
rule-level gate looked like it separated by 3.38pp; after it, by 0.22pp. The gate was always the
wrong sign for a product and is now also visibly flat — which is what §141 argued and what the
defect had been hiding behind a number that looked like a signal.

The shares over rows and over sentences now sit beside each other in the artefact (13.98% and
14.0%), which is the check that the counting unit does not decide the verdict. It does not.

**Green.** `pnpm eval:rule-form` writes `poc-rule-form.json` from the same committed artefact as
§140, §141 and §143, calls no model, and runs in `pnpm check`. `rule-form.ts` and the extended
`diff-corpus.ts` are at **100 on all four coverage dimensions**; 2,397 tests; `99.98 / 99.66 / 100
/ 99.98`. CI asserts the two new pool counts and the agreement of the two naming shares, so an
id-keyed lookup cannot come back quietly.

**One rule the audit caught on me.** The new reading printed with `console.log`, which this
repository forbids in non-test code and enforces with `pnpm audit:repo`. It failed the build, which
is the check working; the fix was `process.stdout.write`, and the delete-the-guard-that-cannot-run
rule was applied to a `throw` in the same file rather than covering it with a test.

## 145 — The question that said the least was damaged the least

R32's third axis was the last candidate standing: *the question is one the schema can answer two
ways — an ambiguity the pack resolves in the wrong direction*. Axes 1 and 2 were closed negatively,
so this was the only account of the mechanism left, and the prediction was that a question which
does not say which columns it needs is the kind a pack damages.

**The measure.** For each question, take the columns the reference query requires and ask how many
of them the question — or the benchmark's external-knowledge block, which a solver may also read —
names outright. Star projections are dropped, because `SELECT count(*)` requires no column and
counting its expansion would report a question as silent about something it never had to say. The
result is four bands: names none of them (131 questions), fewer than half (444), most but not all
(778), all of them (181).

**The result is the opposite of the prediction.**

| what the question named | n | Δ vs no memory | baseline correct | destroyed | repaired |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **none of its columns** | 131 | **+4.58pp** | 57.3% | **1.33%** | 12.50% |
| fewer than half | 444 | +0.90pp | 60.4% | 6.72% | 12.50% |
| most but not all | 778 | −0.26pp | 53.5% | **8.41%** | 9.12% |
| all of them | 181 | −1.66pp | 67.4% | 6.56% | 8.47% |

The raw deltas fall monotonically across the four bands, which on its own reads like a finding and
is not one: the baselines move with them, from 57.3% to 67.4%, and a question that starts correct
has more to lose. `destroyed` is the conditional rate the comparison has to use — the share of
already-correct queries the pack broke — and it reverses the picture. **The band that named nothing
is destroyed at a sixth of the rate of the band that named most.** The ambiguity axis predicted the
opposite and is refuted.

**And it is not a difficulty effect, which is what the strata are for.** A question that names
nothing is plausibly also a harder one, so every reading is taken inside the benchmark's own label:

| difficulty | none | few | most | all |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| simple | 1.54% (107) | 7.34% (278) | 7.56% (412) | 6.52% (128) |
| moderate | 0.00% (18) | 2.74% (130) | **10.53%** (273) | 8.00% (43) |
| challenging | — (6) | 16.67% (36) | 6.67% (93) | — (10) |

Both strata with enough questions say the same thing and the moderate one says it more loudly.
Challenging has 6 questions in its smallest band and cannot be read; it is reported rather than
dropped because dropping it would leave the impression that every stratum agreed.

### What R32 leaves

All three axes are closed and all three are negative:

| axis | verdict | the number that decided it |
|---|---|---|
| the pack changed the table set | **inert** — the imported name counted twice | 45.2% overlap, 0.00pp outside it (§143) |
| the rule is procedural rather than declarative | **unmeasurable** — the classes are not distinct | 57.9% of sentences carry both marker kinds (§144) |
| the question is one the schema can answer two ways | **refuted** — the direction is backwards | 1.33% destroyed where nothing is named against 8.41% where most is (§145) |

R32's own refutation clause applies, and it was written before any of these numbers existed: *if no
feature separates, the honest conclusion is that this corpus cannot attribute the damage to anything
in the pack, and the product statement narrows to the read-time check with no account of its cause —
which is a usable product and an incomplete science, and would be reported as both.*

That is what is reported. The one stable separation in this corpus is still §140's — a query that
introduces an ungrounded name is worth −11.13pp and nothing else survives its own half-width — and
§141 already showed that the rule's *text* cannot predict which queries those will be. Three
structural accounts of the mechanism have now been tested and three have failed. **The mechanism is
not attributable from this corpus's structure, and the read-time check remains the deliverable.**

**Green.** `pnpm eval:referent` writes `poc-referent.json` from the same committed artefact as the
rest of R32 and runs in `pnpm check`; CI recomputes it, compares bytes and asserts 11 numbers,
including that the simple and moderate strata each independently refuse the prediction. `referent.ts`
is at **100 on all four coverage dimensions**; 2,412 tests; `99.98 / 99.63 / 100 / 99.98`.

## 146 — Out of sample, memory costs 0.71pp and the gate recovers 72% of it

R30 stage 2 ran on 2026-11-01 (`41296776252`, 10:18Z–11:25Z, **14,479 model calls**, 2 retries, 0
timeouts) over **7,000 questions in 58 databases that neither dev nor Mini-Dev contains**. Every
prediction in `prereg/R30-stage2.md` was written before the dispatch. Four of the five arrived; the
one that did not is the most informative thing in this section.

**The run is measurable, and that is the first thing to check rather than the last.** All twelve
gates passed: 7,000 of 7,000 questions evaluated exactly once with no leaks, gold 100% executable,
parse 99.97%, execution 98.19%, minimum detectable effect **0.82pp** against the 0.94pp registered.
The instrument did what it was bought for. Nothing below is a measurement of the harness.

**And the effect is smaller than that resolution.** 0.71pp against 0.82pp, so `eval:power` files this
artefact as *within 95% but under 80% power* — the same category it gives four of the seventeen earlier
runs, and the category this record has never upgraded for being the interesting one. The direction and
the significance are established: the interval excludes zero, five folds agree, McNemar p = 0.0172.
The **magnitude** sits at the edge of what 7,000 questions were sized to see, and a claim that quoted
−0.71pp as though the sample had settled its size would be doing the thing §141 was withdrawn for.

| | dev (in-sample) | **train (out of sample)** |
|---|---|---|
| questions | 1,534 | **7,000** |
| databases | 11 | **58** |
| accuracy, no memory | 57.43% | 58.21% |
| accuracy, with memory | 57.76% | 57.50% |
| **delta** | **+0.33pp** | **−0.71pp** |
| interval, questions resampled | [−1.11, +1.76] | [−1.30, −0.13] |
| **interval, databases resampled** | **[−0.63, +1.36]** | **[−1.27, −0.18]** |
| lost / gained | 62 / 67 | **237 / 187** |
| McNemar p | 0.7249 | **0.0172** |
| `eval:power` category | underpowered | **within 95% but under 80% power** |

**The clustered interval is the one that decides this.** §143 closed R32's first axis by insisting
that questions inside a database are not independent, and the headline of this round had never been
through that check: `comparePaired` resamples questions. Recomputed with the database as the unit,
the interval is [−1.27, −0.18] — narrower on this corpus, not wider, and still excluding zero. The
harm survives the correction that killed the earlier claim, which is the only reason it is reported
as harm rather than as an unresolved wobble.

**Five folds, five negatives.** −1.21, −0.93, −0.50, −0.71, −0.21. Each fold learns its own store
from its own 280 questions and never sees the questions it is scored on, so these are five nearly
independent replications and not one measurement split five ways. The exact two-sided sign test is
**p = 0.0625**, which is the floor a five-fold test can reach: unanimity cannot clear 0.05 at this
number of folds. That is a limit of the design, recorded rather than rounded away, and it is why the
bootstrap interval rather than the sign test carries the claim.

### The harm is not spread over the corpus; it is in 7.8% of it

`F1` — the memory query imported a name that neither the question nor the baseline query mentions —
is the covariate §140 found and §141 tried to explain. On train it is **548 questions, 7.8% of the
corpus**, and the arithmetic of the whole round sits in one row:

| cohort | n | helped | harmed | net | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| imported a name | 548 (7.8%) | 40 | 76 | **−36** | **−6.57pp** |
| left the query alone | 6,452 (92.2%) | 147 | 161 | −14 | −0.22pp |
| whole corpus | 7,000 | 187 | 237 | **−50** | −0.71pp |

**72% of the net harm is carried by 7.8% of the questions.** The gap between the cohorts is −6.35pp
against a clustered interval of [−10.99, −1.92], p = 0.0158: it resolves out of sample, on a corpus
whose databases dev has never seen. That is the strongest single result this project has produced,
and it is a result about a *failure*, not a success.

### The gate recovers most of it, and the product still does not pay

Discarding those 548 questions and scoring each from the no-memory query the record already holds —
a column, not a prediction — moves the arm from **−0.71pp to −0.20pp**: the filter is worth
**+0.51pp**. It is stable on all three readings: leave-one-database-out 0.45pp to 0.62pp across 58
databases, split-half 0.68pp / 0.34pp, and a permutation null of 0.06pp [−0.10, 0.21] at
**p = 0.0002**. Discarding the same number of questions at random buys 0.06pp; the placement is what
the gate is.

And then the number that matters for the product: **−0.20pp is not distinguishable from zero.** On
dev the gated arm read +1.30pp. On train it reads −0.20pp, so *memory plus the gate is not better
than not using memory at all*, and memory without the gate is measurably worse.

> **The product statement on dev was "the read-time filter turns a wash into +1.30pp". Out of sample
> it is "the filter recovers 72% of what memory costs, leaving no net gain".** That is the honest
> sentence and it is the sentence the documentation now carries.

### Four predictions held and the fifth is the interesting one

| | registered | observed | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P1** | the run is measurable | 12/12 gates, gold 100%, mde 0.82pp | **held** |
| **P2** | the full arm is not positive **and not significantly different** from none | −0.71pp, clustered [−1.27, −0.18] | **refuted** |
| **P3** | the gate is worth between +0.2pp and +2.0pp | **+0.51pp** | held, at the low end |
| **P4** | shrinkage of less than half: a point estimate in [0.49, 0.98] | **+0.51pp**, 52% retained | **held** |
| **P5** | an imported identifier is still a negative covariate | −6.57pp against −0.22pp | **held** |

**P2 was written to be the safe prediction and it is the one that failed.** On dev the mechanism
never moved raw accuracy — +0.33pp [−1.11, +1.76] — and the registration expected that to hold. It
does not: out of sample the memory arm is *worse*, and the interval excludes zero. The prediction was
not about a mechanism this project had not tested; it was about a number this project had measured
once and generalised. That is what an out-of-sample test is for, and it cost one line of a
pre-registration to make the failure legible.

**P4 landed with 0.02pp of margin.** The registration said a point estimate below +0.49pp would mean
the dev figure was carried by the corpus, and anything in [0.49, 0.98] would be shrinkage of the size
an out-of-sample test is supposed to produce. The reading is **+0.51pp**. A narrower band would have
refuted; a wider one would have proved nothing. It is the one prediction in this record whose
boundary was set tightly enough to have failed and did not.

### The explanation does not survive, and the filter does

§141 said the damage is where the *pack's own text* introduced the name. That account does not
replicate, and the three numbers that say so are independent of each other:

| | dev | train |
|---|---|---|
| imported names the pack's text accounts for (exact) | 60 of 155, **38.7%** | 107 of 548, **19.5%** |
| the same, forgiving spelling (flattened) | 81 of 155, **52.3%** | 163 of 548, **29.7%** |
| pack stratum against schema stratum | −8.33pp vs −9.57pp | −6.54pp vs −5.83pp |
| gap between those strata | −1.24pp, unresolved | **−0.72pp ± 10.76, unresolved** |
| share of the gate's +0.51pp from questions the pack named | — | **0.10pp of 0.51pp (19.4%)** |

**The attribution halves and the mechanism splits stop resolving.** On train, 75% of the imported
names are real schema columns the question never asked for: the model reached into the schema it was
shown, not into the rule text. Only a fifth of the gate's benefit comes from questions whose pack
named anything at all.

**So the filter is a property of the query, not of the pack.** That is a correction to §141 and it is
the useful one: the gate does not need to know what the rules said, only what the generated query
did. A rule that names nothing can still push the model into over-specifying, and the case where the
pack named the column is the minority of the harm rather than its definition.

### This is the field's failure mode, not this project's

The negative effect is not idiosyncratic. Three external results say the same thing with different
machinery, and they were found after the measurement rather than used to design it:

- **CTIM-Rover** (Lindenbauer, Groh & Schütze, `arXiv:2505.23422`) added cross-task memory to
  AutoCodeRover and reported resolution falling from 42% to 31% in its memory-only configuration on a
  45-issue SWE-bench Verified subset. Its diagnosis is that memory acts as surface-level noise
  biasing the agent's first steps — supported by the fact that inserting an arbitrary item
  ("GRANDMA LIKES PASTA") *restored* success, which rules out "the memory was wrong" and leaves
  "the memory was there".
- **Xiong et al. (2025)** name the mechanism *experience-following*: the more similar a new task is to
  a retrieved memory, the more the output resembles that memory's output. Benefit and harm both come
  from the same reflex.
- **LongMemEval** (Wu et al., ICLR 2025) measures commercial assistants losing about 30% on tasks that
  require updating a remembered fact, and **MemEvoBench** (Xie et al., 2026) calls the drift *memory
  misevolution*, finding static prompt-level defences insufficient — the fix has to be structural.

**What microglia adds to that list is a magnitude and a location.** The field says cross-task memory
can hurt; this record says by how much (0.71pp of execution accuracy at 7,000 questions), where it
sits (7.8% of questions, 72% of the net harm), what it looks like in the output (a name the question
never asked for), and how much a query-level filter recovers (72% of the cost, stable at p = 0.0002).
CTIM-Rover's "surface-level noise" and this record's "the pack does not have to name the column" are
the same claim from two directions, and this one has a per-question footprint.

### Two defects, both caught by looking at an output rather than at a diff

**The stability reading described itself wrongly when pointed at the new corpus.** Its title was a
constant — `Whether the read-time gate's +1.30pp is …`, which is dev's number — and its `unmeasured`
block asserted that *"every question here was in the corpus that produced §140, so no split of it is
out of sample"*. True of dev; the exact negation of what the train split is for. The artefact then
reported a correctly measured 0.51pp under a heading that denied the measurement, and no check looked
at prose. Fixed by deriving every corpus-dependent clause from the corpus: `splitOfName` reads the
artefact's own `dataset` field, `stabilityFramingOf` builds the title from the number it read and the
database count it counted, and the caveat becomes the *causal* one over an out-of-sample split
because the in-sample one would be false. Seven tests pin the construction, including that the title
does not contain a number the reading did not produce.

**The headline interval did not match the unit of observation.** `comparePaired` resamples questions
while §143's own lesson, quoted three sections earlier in this file, is that questions inside a
database are not independent. The out-of-sample claim is now reported with the database as the
resampling unit; the question-level interval is kept in the source artefact and the difference is
0.03pp, which is why it changes nothing here — and is exactly why it would have gone unnoticed.

**Both are the same shape as the three in AUDIT §29:** not a crash, a plausible number. 2,445 tests
and 99.98 / 99.64 / 100 / 99.98 coverage did not catch either, because both were statements about a
corpus rather than computations over one.

## 147 — The pack repairs almost as much as it breaks, and the filter realises 15% of what a perfect one would

**"Memory costs 0.71pp" is one number, and the corpus contains two.** Split the same 7,000 questions by
what memory *did* rather than by what it was worth, and the two directions turn out to be nearly the same
size:

| | questions | of which | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| the bare attempt was wrong, memory repaired it | 2,925 | **187** | **6.39%** |
| the bare attempt was right, memory broke it | 4,075 | **237** | **5.82%** |
| net | 7,000 | **−50** | **−0.71pp** |

**Per question, help is the likelier outcome. Per corpus, harm wins.** Both are true and the reason is
the base: 4,075 questions could only be harmed and 2,925 could only be helped, so a lower rate on the
larger base outweighs a higher rate on the smaller one. The exchange rate — repairs per break — is
**0.79** out of sample.

**This is not a shape that only appears out of sample, and that is the part that matters.** Dev repairs
**10.26%** of 653 and breaks **7.04%** of 881; its exchange rate is **1.08**. Both rates are the same
order of magnitude on both corpora, and both directions are present on both. What crossed one is the
ratio, not the mechanism. §146 said the mechanism does not transfer; this sharpens it — the mechanism is
*there* out of sample at full strength, in both directions at once, and it is losing by a base it does not
control. A story where the rules stop working on a foreign corpus is wrong. A story where they work
equally in both directions and the corpus happens to contain more right answers to break is what the
matrix says.

**Which moves the question from "is memory good" to "can a filter see the breaks".** A filter that removed
exactly the 237 broken questions and none of the 187 repairs would be worth **3.39pp**. The read-time gate
this record has been carrying since §140 removes **548** questions: it catches **76 of 237** breaks
(**32.1%**) and gives up **40 of 187** repairs (**21.4%**), for a net **36** — **15.2 questions discarded
per net error prevented**, and **15.2%** of the ceiling realised.

**And it was never better than that in sample.** On dev the same filter spends **10.3** questions per net
error and realises **24.2%** of a 4.04pp ceiling. The gate has been buying a fifth of its available gain
for as long as this record has had a gate; the out-of-sample run did not introduce a pathology, it removed
the corpus that was forgiving enough to hide one. §140's `+0.51pp` was always 15% of the thing it could
have been.

### What that does to the three shapes R33 is choosing between

**"Ship memory plus the filter" is now bounded above by a wash, not merely measured at one.** Even a
perfect filter can only remove the 237 breaks; it cannot add a repair. On this corpus that makes the best
achievable product *exactly* no-memory accuracy, and the realised product is −0.20pp. The bound and the
measurement agree, which means the −0.20pp is not a tuning shortfall — it is the shape of the mechanism.

**"Ship the filter alone" does not depend on any of this, and that is now its main argument.** The filter
is a query-level validity check: it discards a statement that imports a name the request never implied.
Nothing about it requires the rules. 0.51pp of it was measured with memory present and the fallback
*already written*, which is the corpus's convenience and not a deployment's — but the check itself is one
comparison against text the caller already has.

**"A weaker injection to raise the clean cohort" would move the wrong term.** §145 established that the
damage concentrates on questions that said the least, and §146 established that the pack's benefit does
not concentrate anywhere. Raising the repair rate is the only thing that would flip the exchange rate, and
nothing in this matrix suggests a dose that raises repairs without raising breaks proportionally — the two
rates have moved together on both corpora measured so far.

### How it was almost missed, which is the transferable part

The counts were in the artefact from the night of the run. `helped: 187, harmed: 237` sat in the same cell
as `deltaPp: −0.71` in `poc-sota-bird-train.json` for as long as the run has existed, and §146 wrote four
thousand words around that cell without dividing the two counts by their own bases — because the base for
each is a *different* denominator, and the artefact reported one delta, so one denominator was all that was
ever in view.

> Two counts in one cell are not a comparison until somebody divides them by the two different things they
> are counts *of*.

The fix is the same as §145's and the same as §146's: make the reading the artefact carries be the reading
the claim needs. `memoryDiscordanceOf` splits by outcome, divides each side by its own base, and prices the
filter against the ceiling it could reach — and `realisedPp` is then `gate.improvementPp` computed from the
confusion matrix instead of by re-reading the corpus with the fallback substituted. One number, two
derivations, and a test that holds them equal: if the two accounts of the filter ever disagree, one of them
is describing a different corpus.

**Nothing in the literature this record compares against would have surfaced it either.** Aggregate deltas
are the standard reporting unit — the memory systems tracked here report end-task accuracy before and after
memory, which is exactly the number that cannot distinguish "repairs as much as it breaks" from "does
nothing". This is not a criticism of those papers; none of them had a negative to explain. It is why the
matrix belongs in the artefact: a mechanism whose two directions are within 0.6pp of each other is
invisible in the only number most evaluations publish.

**Where this leaves the programme.** Not with a better memory — with a precise statement of what a filter
would have to do. The gate's problem was never coverage; it catches fewer than a third of the breaks and
pays for each catch with a fifth of a repair. Any successor has to move precision, and the ceiling it is
working against is 3.39pp, which is small enough that it should be decided before it is engineered.

## 148 — Pointed at one query, the filter flags 95% of everything and sorts almost nothing

**R33 stage 0 cost no model call, and it closed a product option.** §146 measured the filter as a
difference between two statements; §147 priced that difference against its ceiling. Neither had asked
the question a deployment without rules would ask: does the *query* carry the signal, or only the
*difference*? `prereg/R33.md` was written before the number, with the rule, both grounding modes, and a
bar taken from the filter itself — Youden's index, `76/237 + 147/187 − 1 = 0.1068`.

| | flag rate | accuracy flagged | accuracy clean | gap | **Youden** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| train, bare, strict | **94.8%** | 57.64% | 70.22% | −12.58pp [−22.15, −2.92] | **0.0257** |
| train, served, strict | 95.2% | 56.91% | 69.44% | −12.52pp | 0.0235 |
| train, bare, morphological | 75.8% | 56.05% | 65.33% | −9.28pp | 0.0700 |
| dev, bare, strict | 93.3% | 55.97% | 77.67% | −21.70pp [−31.03, −12.08] | 0.0556 |
| dev, bare, morphological | 74.3% | 52.59% | 71.39% | −18.80pp | 0.1470 |
| *the diff-anchored filter* | *7.8%* | — | — | — | ***0.1068*** |

**The rule fires on almost everything, for a reason that is structural rather than statistical.** A
correct query names tables and columns that no question spells out — `u2base`, `movieid`, `rating` for
"rated" — so a grounding rule anchored on the question alone is measuring the *schema vocabulary*, not
an imported name. Where §146's covariate subtracted the bare query first, this one has nothing to
subtract, and 94.8% of attempts are flagged.

**The gap it shows is real and is not about the rule.** Flagged attempts are 12.58pp less accurate on an
interval that excludes zero. But 94.8% of the corpus is inside that group, and the 5.2% outside it are
the questions whose table names appear in their own text — which is a proxy for an easy question, not for
a valid one. Youden is the statistic that removes the base rate, and it reads **0.0257**: a quarter of the
filter it would replace, and below what a coin flip plus the base rate would be worth.

**The morphological arm was the sensitivity analysis, written before the result.** Loosening the rule to
accept inflected identifiers cuts the flag rate by 19 points and lifts Youden to **0.0700** — still under
0.1068. That forecloses the obvious next move ("the tokeniser is the problem") for the price of a column
in a table, which is the only reason to register a second rule before seeing either.

### What the flag rate could not show, and the clean group could

P6 asked whether the pack still imports names when the anchor is gone: served flagged minus bare flagged.
It returned **+0.42pp** and it was never going to return anything else — with 94.8% of bare attempts
already flagged, the entire population the difference can move within is 5.2 points wide. That is a
defect in the registration, not in the corpus (AUDIT §31.2).

Asked on the population that has room, it answers:

| | questions the bare rule passes | the pack imports a name on | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| train | 1,693 | 99 | **5.8%** |
| dev | 395 | 24 | **6.1%** |

**That is §146's imported-name finding reproduced under a second, independent rule.** §146 found 7.8% of
served queries importing a name the bare one did not; this finds 5.8% of the *clean* questions acquiring
one from the pack, with the anchor removed and only the question as context. The mechanism is not an
artefact of how the covariate was anchored. **It is the only positive result this stage produced**, and
it is the reason the negative is credible: the same rule that fails as a standalone check succeeds at
detecting what the pack does.

### What it does to R33's three shapes

| shape | before §147–§148 | now |
|---|---|---|
| 1. ship the check alone | the only option that does not depend on the rules | **refuted as specified.** The check is differential, so a deployment has to generate twice and compare. That is a real cost, and paying it buys a filter worth 0.51pp against a 3.39pp ceiling |
| 2. ship memory + filter | measured at −0.20pp | **bounded above by a wash**: a perfect filter removes breaks and cannot add repairs (§147) |
| 3. a weaker injection | untested | **still untested, and now the only open one** — but nothing measured suggests a dose that raises repairs without raising breaks |

So the programme's product question is closed in the honest direction: **nothing ships.** The remaining
work is not a product decision but a research one — whether an injection exists that moves the repair
rate without moving the break rate — and it should be registered as such rather than resuming as a
feature.

### The six registrations, as adjudicated

| | claim | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | both corpora load, every missing query is one the run records as a failure | **holds** — 10 bare and 2 served missing, all consistent (AUDIT §31.1) |
| P2 | the strict rule flags ≥60% and the loose one ≥40% of bare attempts | **holds** — 94.8% and 75.8% |
| P3 | flagged attempts are ≥5pp less accurate on an interval excluding zero | **holds** — −12.58pp [−22.15, −2.92] |
| P4 | dev's gap is within 4pp of train's | **refuted** — −21.70pp against −12.58pp, same sign, nine points apart |
| P5 | Youden clears the filter's 0.1068 on both splits | **refuted** — 0.0257 and 0.0556 |
| P6 | the pack adds ≥5pp of flag rate | **refuted** — +0.42pp, and unreachable by construction |

**Two predictions were refuted and one of them was unfalsifiable in practice.** P6's bar could not be
reached under P2's own floor, which is the kind of thing a registration is supposed to prevent and did
not: the mistake was writing a pair of predictions as independent claims about one corpus. That is
recorded in AUDIT §31.2 rather than repaired in place, and the conditional quantity that replaces it —
5.8% of clean questions — is in the artefact beside the number it corrects.

### Two defects, both found by a gate written before the data was read

**Ten of 7,000 rows out of sample carry no bare query.** `V53` failed on first run; the ten are ordinary
rows that simply never stored `baselineSql`, and every reading that touches the field treats it as an
operand rather than a subject, so an empty one produced a plausible zero. Their treatment moved the gap
from −12.58pp to −10.71pp and the interval across zero — one verdict flipped on ten rows, which is why
Amendment 1 publishes both columns.

**A registered threshold the registration made unreachable.** P2's floor and P6's difference could not
jointly hold at the flag rate the rule actually produces. The arithmetic was available before the file
was written and was not done.

**Both are the same shape** — a quantity never given a denominator, or a field never asked about on its
own. 2,489 tests and four coverage dimensions at 99.98 / 99.64 / 100 / 99.98 did not catch either,
because both were questions about the corpus rather than computations over it.

## 149 — The memory is not close to a wash; it is 43% short, and the population cannot be reselected either

**R34 cost no model call and closed the last open shape.** §147 measured the exchange rate and §148 closed
two of R33's three shapes, leaving "a weaker injection" as a research question. That framing was wrong, and
the arithmetic says so before any new number: a repair can only happen on a question the bare model got
wrong and a break only on one it got right, so the two rates sit on different bases and **the exchange rate
at which memory breaks even is the odds of the bare model being right, not parity.**

| quantity | value | derivation |
|---|---|---|
| repairable / breakable | 2,925 / 4,075 | §147 |
| repaired / broken | 187 (6.393%) / 237 (5.816%) | §147 |
| exchange rate | **0.789** | 187 / 237 |
| **break-even exchange rate** | **1.393** | 4,075 / 2,925 |
| clearance | **0.566** | 0.789 / 1.393 |
| repairs needed at fixed breaks | **8.10%**, +1.71pp | 5.816% × 1.393 |
| breaks needed at fixed repairs | **4.59%**, −1.23pp | 6.393% / 1.393 |

**Every "close to a wash" in this record was measured against the wrong zero.** Twenty-one per cent short
became forty-three, and the two ways out are now numbers rather than rhetoric: raise repairs to 8.10% at
fixed breaks, or cut breaks to 4.59% at fixed repairs. Nothing this programme has built has come within a
point of either.

### The shape was mis-specified: the variable is the population, not the dose

A question the bare model already answered cannot be repaired; a question it got wrong cannot be broken.
Admit memory only to the second kind and the break rate is **zero by construction**, so the whole 6.39%
repair rate arrives as net gain — **+2.67pp**, the largest figure in this record and the first one in front
of the memory rather than behind it. That is a different mechanism from the read-time filter: the filter
removes breaks *after* generation and is capped at 3.39pp; admission avoids them *before* it and is capped
at the repair rate. The two ceilings are the halves of a **6.06pp** oracle, and §147 had published only the
second half.

The gate does not have to be good, only better than random. Net gain on the corpus is
`τ · (q·r − (1−q)·b)`, positive when `q > b / (r + b)` = **47.64%** against a **41.79%** base rate — a
5.85pp lift. That is a far lower bar than the filter's Youden of 0.1068, and it is why the shape was worth
one more round rather than a concession.

`prereg/R34.md` fixed five gates and a split before the numbers existed: SKR's kNN signal in lexical form
(the share of a question's ten nearest neighbours **in the same database** that the bare model got wrong,
leave-one-out, ties broken by id), the pack's coverage of the question in both directions, a two-item dose
split, their conjunction, and a seeded random control. 58 databases dealt 29/29 by a stable hash; thresholds
swept over six quantiles **on the discovery half only**; the selected rule evaluated unchanged on the other.

### What the gate did, and the part the registration did not anticipate

| gate | coverage | precision (needs 47.6%) | confirmation gain | interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| self-knowledge, t = 0.50 | 35.6% | **62.4%** | **−0.05pp** | [−0.50, +0.45] |
| coverage-high, t = 0.182 | 25.6% | 44.9% | −0.11pp | [−0.55, +0.35] |
| coverage-low, t = 0 | 23.2% | 28.3% | −0.19pp | [−0.55, +0.16] |
| pack ≥ 2 items | 93.6% | 39.7% | −0.69pp | [−1.33, −0.08] |
| conjunction, t = 0.30 | 18.4% | 54.0% | **+0.08pp** | [−0.30, +0.50] |
| *best of all 30 points* | *14.8%* | *58.5%* | ***+0.11pp*** | *[−0.19, +0.44]* |

**The primary gate beat the bar by 14.7pp and lost money.** 62.4% precision against 47.6% asked for, and
−0.05pp on an interval that covers zero — a 20.6pp lift, three and a half times what the registration said
would be enough, and nothing to show for it. The arithmetic was not wrong about the arithmetic. It was
wrong about what the arithmetic is about.

**The precision bar belongs to the admitted set, and selection moves it.**

| threshold | coverage | precision q | bar `b/(r+b)` inside the set | gap | repair rate | break rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | 94.5% | 41.8% | 46.5% | −4.7pp | 6.32% | 5.50% |
| 0.20 | 81.9% | 45.1% | 48.7% | −3.6pp | 6.39% | 6.07% |
| 0.30 | 64.5% | 50.8% | 52.3% | −1.5pp | 6.23% | 6.84% |
| 0.40 | 49.1% | 56.2% | 57.0% | −0.8pp | 5.86% | 7.77% |
| 0.50 | 35.6% | 62.4% | 63.3% | −0.9pp | 5.61% | 9.68% |

Precision climbs 20.6pp across the sweep; the bar climbs 16.8pp with it, and the gap narrows from 4.7pp to
0.8pp and then stops. The reason is in the last two columns: **the break rate inside the admitted set nearly
doubles while the repair rate does not move.** A question whose neighbours were answered wrongly is not a
question the pack can repair — it is a question the model is *unstable* on, and an unstable answer is one
the pack breaks as easily as it fixes. The gate is selecting **variance**, and variance is symmetric, which
is the same property that makes memory a wash in the first place. Selecting on it cannot be a fix for it.

### Two predictions refuted, one of them by the file rather than by the corpus

P5 fails as registered: the interval covers zero and the precision clause is met and irrelevant. P7 —
confirmation at most 70% of discovery — fails because the discovery gain is −0.19pp, so the inequality
inverts and a *better* confirmation half is recorded as a failure. The prediction was written for a positive
effect and no rule had one. It is left refuted rather than repaired: the meaningful content, that an
in-sample rule loses most of its value out of sample, has nothing to test when there was no value to lose.

**Three amendments, and all three are thresholds written without arithmetic.**

| | registered | why it could not work | amended |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P1** | 240 of 424 discordant per half | two halves cannot hold 480 of 424 | 150; both halves clear at 208 and 216 |
| **P3** | within 0.15pp of `τ × net` | at 15% coverage the net's sampling error is ±0.26pp | expected value inside the reading's own clustered interval; 6 of 6 pass |
| **P5** | a gate needs 47.64% precision | the bar is the *admitted set's* `b/(r+b)`, not the corpus's | reported beside every point; verdict unchanged |

That is §147's P6, §31.2's unreachable threshold, and these three — **four registered numbers in two weeks
that no run could have satisfied or that measured the wrong population.** The registration process is now
producing thresholds faster than it checks them, and AUDIT §32 names the family.

### What it closes, and the only thing it leaves

Admission puts 2.67pp above the memory; five gates and thirty registered points reach **+0.11pp** of it out
of sample, **4.0%**, on an interval covering zero. §147's filter realised **15.2%** of its own ceiling and
did not pay. So the removal route was four times as efficient, and both routes fail, for the same underlying
reason: **the effect the intervention produces is symmetric, and every mechanism that could break the
symmetry has to see something about the question that is not in the question.**

Three of R33's shapes are now closed by measurement rather than by argument — the item's content (§145), its
quantity (§146, R16), and the population's selection (§149). What is left is not a fourth gate. It is the
store: R13's 22 of 100 admitted rules, R15's 24 of 102 with no home database, R33's 19.5% of flagged names
traceable to a rule. **The measurement that would send the programme back there with a number now exists, and
it is 43% away from break-even rather than 21%.**

## 150 — The store's items have no value that travels, and the pack size is the only lever left

**R35 cost no model call and closed the store.** §149 closed the population and left one item on the
product list: whether the store's *rules* are worth different amounts, which is what any pruning
intervention presupposes. The answer is that they are different and that the difference does not travel,
and the round found the first real structure in the store while proving it worthless.

### The unit, before the question

Attribution is not exclusive — a flip is credited to every rule in the prompt — so 7,000 questions are
**13,578 injections**: 349 naming a repaired question, 462 a broken one, against 424 flips. Every number
below is per injection, and `store-report.ts` had already written the unit down for the same reason.

### Heterogeneity is real, and the null is the design

| | value |
|---|---|
| rules that reached a prompt | 203 |
| injections | 13,578 |
| χ² dispersion, repair counts | **293.3** |
| permutation null: mean / 99th percentile | **209.6** / 280.4 |
| p | **0.0047** |

The null permutes *outcomes across questions* while every rule keeps exactly the questions it was shown
on. That is the only null that separates "this rule is different" from "these two rules shared a prompt",
and it is why the result is a finding rather than an artefact of pack size.

### And it does not replicate, which is the whole story

| | value |
|---|---|
| rules compared (≥ 5 showings in each half) | 135 |
| split-half correlation of per-rule net rate | **−0.134** [−0.296, +0.036] |
| sign agreement, over the 53 rules that moved twice | **49.1%** |
| Spearman–Brown, full length | **−0.309** |

A **negative** reliability is not "no signal" — it is a signal whose second measurement would be better
inverted. So the heterogeneity is an interaction between a rule and a database: 203 rules × 58 schemas is
11,774 cells over 424 flips, and that is not a table anyone can learn from 7,000 questions.

**The actionable form fails too.** A flag a deployment could actually run — negative net over at least
ten showings — selects 58 rules covering 2,545 of the 3,770 confirmation questions, and those returned
**−0.55pp** against **−0.49pp** for the rest: a difference of **−0.06pp** on [−1.97, +1.56]. Not a weaker
ledger; no signal.

### The one variable that moves is not the content

| pack | questions | repaired | broken | net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| one rule | 423 | 25 / 200 = 12.50% | 12 / 223 = 5.38% | **+3.07pp** |
| two rules | 6,576 | 162 / 2,725 = 5.94% | 225 / 3,851 = 5.84% | −0.96pp |

**+4.03pp [+0.76, +6.62]**, clustered by database. It is registered as a lead, not a finding, for two
reasons that are both in the artefact: retrieval assigns pack size (the singleton questions are harder —
47.3% unanswerable by the bare model against 41.4%), and the same contrast recomputed on every committed
artefact is negative in **12 of 17**:

| corpus | questions | single-rule questions | difference | interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| train | 6,999 | 423 | **+4.03pp** | [+0.76, +6.62] |
| dev, R24 split | 1,534 | 343 | +4.14pp | [+0.83, +6.28] |
| dev, R25 dose | 1,534 | 401 | +3.13pp | [+0.62, +5.23] |
| dev, R26 channels | 1,534 | 380 | +0.62pp | [−1.74, +2.95] |
| dev | 1,534 | 97 | +0.36pp | [−2.40, +3.45] |
| twelve 350-question pilots | 350 each | 33–78 | −1.55 to −13.98pp | 3 of 12 exclude zero, negatively |

Every artefact above a thousand questions is positive, every pilot is negative, and the split is what a
**sample-size** explanation predicts exactly: the pilots hold 33–78 singleton questions, the full splits
97–423. Three pilot intervals do exclude zero in the negative direction, which is why this stays a lead
rather than being dismissed.

### What it changes

Four routes had been closed while holding the corpus fixed. This is the fifth, and it is the strongest
form the negative has taken: **a rule has no per-item value that transfers, so a store cannot be improved
by editing its items one at a time.** Two levers remain and both are designs — the **grain** at which
memory is written, and the **number of items a prompt carries**. R36 is the second one, and it is cheap:
the arm assigns pack size instead of observing it, and one rule per prompt halves the prompt tokens of
the run it replaces.

Sealed by 2,572 tests (40 new), four coverage dimensions at 99.98 / 99.66 / 100 / 99.98 with the new
module at 100% on all four, 24 new CI assertions, and three gates (`V59`–`V61`).

## 151 — The pack size was the questions, and removing an item is not a subtraction

**The lead R35 registered was already measured, and the measurement says no.** R35 left one number above
zero: questions whose pack held a single rule outscored questions whose pack held two by **+4.03pp
[+0.76, +6.62]** on the train corpus and +3.13pp on dev, recorded as a lead because retrieval assigns pack
size. The arm that assigns it has existed since R25 — `full-one`, the same retrieval cut to its first item,
on every question — and R25 reported it as a *dose control* rather than as a test. Re-read as the test:

| | value |
|---|---|
| `full-one` − `full`, dev, clustered by database | **−0.33pp [−1.65, +1.25]**, 42 gained / 47 lost, p = 0.6718 |
| the lane's own `arm_pairs` entry for the same pair | −0.33pp, 42/47 — the recount agrees to a hundredth of a point |
| R35's observed contrast on the same split | +3.13pp [+0.87, +5.23] recomputed at the default 2,000 resamples |
| clearance of the 1-item pack / of the 2-item pack | **0.672** / **0.737**, on a hurdle of 1.335 |

**Where the +3.13pp came from, in one table.** The two populations differ in break rate, not in repair rate:

| pack | questions | repaired of repairable | broken of breakable |
|---|---|---|---|
| one rule | 401 | 18 of 189 (**9.5%**) | **9 of 212 (4.2%)** |
| two rules | 1,133 | 42 of 468 (**9.0%**) | **52 of 665 (7.8%)** |

Singleton questions are questions where the store had one relevant thing to say, and a store that says one
thing breaks half as often. Handing the second population the first population's pack size does not hand it
the first population's break rate — it hands back 27 breaks and 23 repairs at the same time.

**The result that outlives the sign: the pack is not additive.** The arms differ by one rule, so the
contrast decomposes into four cells, and two of them point the other way:

| the question was… | pair right | pair wrong | |
|---|---|---|---|
| one the bare model missed | 23 | 15 | the second rule repairs 23, and **prevents 15** the single rule would have repaired |
| one the bare model answered | 24 | 27 | it **prevents 24** breaks, and causes 27 |

The second rule's own record is 23 repairs against 27 breaks — **0.85 per break**, a net harm, which is
exactly what R35's contrast appeared to license removing. It also prevents 15 repairs and 24 breaks: the
first rule answers differently when it is alone in the block. The four cells sum to the measured −5
questions, and that identity is a unit test rather than a remark. **So "how many rules fit" is not a dial:
the marginal item's effect depends on which items are already there**, and every knob that moves the count —
a character budget, a top-k, a density threshold — is tuning an interaction it cannot see.

**Two defects found on the way, both recorded rather than smoothed.**

1. **The dev archival manifest never declared its nested archive.** `dev.zip` ships `dev_databases.zip`
   inside `dev_20240627/`, and `bird-dev.json` named the outer archive's root and nothing about the nest. A
   dev dispatch therefore downloaded 346 MB, verified the digest, unpacked a directory holding only a zip,
   and failed on the first question — the failure the manifest field exists to prevent, in the one split
   that had never been through the code path that reads it. Fixed, pinned by a test that states all three
   splits' layouts, and turned into a single pre-flight that names the missing field (`AUDIT` §34.1).
2. **R35's published dev interval was computed at 400 resamples.** The point estimate reproduces exactly
   (+3.13pp) and the upper bound to 0.004pp; the lower bound is +0.62 in `ROADMAP.md` and +0.87 here,
   because that one row was produced at a fifth of the resample count the rest of the round used. Nothing
   in R35's conclusion turns on it, and the row is restated at the default (`AUDIT` §34.2).

**The replication, and the fold that looked decided.** The dispatch this round registered landed on a fresh
store draw of the same split — 4,970 calls, `learn_sample = 280`, the same five folds — and it reads
**−0.07pp [−1.34, +1.20]**, 38 gained against 39 lost. **P5 holds**: the upper bound is 0.80pp inside the 2pp
bar the file fixed before the run. Every qualitative fact about the marginal item repeats too, which matters
more than the pooled number:

| | first store (R25) | second store (R36) |
|---|---|---|
| `full-one` − `full`, clustered | −0.33pp [−1.65, +1.25] | **−0.07pp [−1.34, +1.20]** |
| the second item's record | 23 repairs / 27 breaks (0.85) | **20 repairs / 23 breaks (0.87)** |
| clearance, one rule / the pair | 0.672 / 0.737 | **0.708 / 0.721** |
| prompts the arm actually changed | 73.9% | 76.2% |

**The per-fold table, read as pairs.** The split is seeded, so fold *k* is the same questions in both
artefacts — 0 of 1,534 questions change fold — which turns the per-fold reading from an inference into a
paired measurement:

| fold | questions | first draw | second draw | sign kept | intervals span zero |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 307 | 0 | −2 | — (zero first) | both |
| 1 | 307 | −4 | −1 | yes | both |
| 2 | 307 | +4 | +5 | yes | both |
| 3 | 307 | **−5** [−2.55, −0.66] | −1 [−2.93, +2.06] | yes | first **no**, second yes |
| 4 | 306 | 0 | −2 | — (zero first) | both |

Three folds keep their sign, and the two that do not are exactly zero on the first draw and have none to
keep. **So the per-fold sign is not drawn anew per store — and that was the sentence this page published an
hour before the replication landed.** What the second draw does take away is the only thing a per-fold table
exists to find: fold 3 is the single row in either draw whose interval excludes zero, and on the second store
it covers zero. The corrected claim is narrower and just as final for the lever: **no fold in either draw
produces an effect distinguishable from noise, and the one that appeared to does not on the second draw.** A
quantity with no decidable fold cannot be calibrated — not because folds disagree, but because none of them
decides. Recorded as `AUDIT` §34.6, together with the process failure that produced it: `foldsOf` shipped
without the interval column that `assignmentOf` had been returning all along.

**What it closes.** Both of R35's remaining levers were designs. The item count is now measured at
**0.672 clearance against 0.737** on one store and **0.708 against 0.721** on a second, and it does not pay
on either. What is left is the **grain** at which memory is written — and the four-cell decomposition says
why that is the right place to look: if removing one item changes what another does, the unit that matters is
what the item *is*, not how many of them fit.

Sealed by 2,615 tests (43 new), four coverage dimensions at 99.98 / 99.66 / 100 / 99.98 with the new
module at **100% on all four**, 32 CI assertions on the reading (8 new), and two gates (`V62`–`V63`) emitted
by the reading rather than by the dispatch. One further defect was caught by the repository's own protocol
check on the push that carried the replication: the registration's `gates` header listed those two and not
the thirteen the dispatch actually emitted, and `eval:protocol` refused it in both directions (`AUDIT`
§34.7). The header now states the dispatch's set; the deciding pair are named with their criteria in the
file, where a reader looking for them will find them.

## 152 — The second scenario's record can now carry four more gates

**R36 closed on two store draws, and the second draw cost 4,970 calls.** The replication read **−0.07pp
[−1.34, +1.20]** on the same 1,534 questions, so P5 held with 0.80pp to spare against the 2pp bar the file fixed
before the run. What repeats is the useful part: the second item is a net harm on both stores (23/27 and 20/23,
0.85 and 0.87 repairs per break) and one rule clears less of the hurdle than the pair on both (0.672/0.737 and
0.708/0.721). What does not repeat is the one fold that looked decided — fold 3's interval excluded zero on the
first draw and covers it on the second — which is why the count lever is closed by *no fold deciding*, not by folds
disagreeing (`AUDIT` §34.6). Two defects were caught on the way in, by the repository's own checks rather than by
reading: the registration's `gates` header claimed a run that never happened (`AUDIT` §34.7) and the power audit did
not yet see the new artefact.

**R29 stage 1 is built and not yet dispatched.** The τ² driver now exports `instrument()`, which returns the arm
record the protocol reads — mean items per pack counted at the facade, the call tally, the learning bookkeeping, the
domain ledger, and the split with its repeats — and `l4` writes it into `poc-l4.json` under `tau2`, which
`pnpm eval:l4-pair` already consumes through `tau2GateAudit`. The arithmetic is a pure function with 8 tests at
100% on four coverage dimensions, deliberately: a mapping that lives inside a driver can only be tested by buying a
dispatch, and a dispatch tests the environment and the arithmetic at once, so a failure cannot be attributed to
either.

**Four numbers in it can be filled dishonestly, and each is refused by name** (`AUDIT` §34.8): an empty pack set
reports 0 rather than "not applicable", because that is V1's failure case; a run that made no call omits `calls`
rather than claiming 0% failures; an unobservable distillation count omits the learning record rather than handing
V32 a perfect score; and the held-out list reaches the gate with its repeats, since V2 asks whether every question
was asked once and a record that tidies its input answers its own question.

**What the dispatch will decide, stated in advance.** Whether the agent's turns are countable at all depends on what
upstream's `SimulationRun` exposes. If they are, stage 1 supplies five of the nine supplyable gates and the ceiling
moves from four informative gates to six; if not, it supplies four and R29's first prediction is refuted in the
direction the prediction was written to detect. Every read in `diagnostics_of` is wrapped so a renamed upstream field
becomes "not observable" rather than a failed benchmark.

**Where this stands.** 2,623 tests across 128 files, four coverage dimensions at 99.98 / 99.66 / 100 / 99.98, both
repositories pushed, CI green on `0c6433e`. The replication is committed as the projection its reader reads — six
per-case columns plus the full metadata — because the sandbox's GitHub route refuses a body above roughly 3 MB, and
the projection was verified to produce a byte-identical reading.

## 153 — The grain is not refused and not tested

**R37 cost one dispatch and changed what a memory item is.** Six routes had been closed with the corpus held
fixed and every one of them changed *which* sentences reached the prompt, how many, or what they were called:
content (§145), quantity (§146), the filter (§147–§148), the population (§149), the store's items (§150), the
item count (§151). This round changed the object. Instead of a sentence of advice about how to build a query, a
**term and what it denotes**, retrieved by the term and rendered only on a question that contains it.

**Why the grain was the right place to look, in one number the record already had.** BIRD attaches a curated
definition to most dev questions — 142 characters, mean. Removing it costs **17.01pp** on the dev split, paired,
clustered (§133). The rule pack on the same split costs **−0.59pp**. Two objects in one prompt slot, and the gap
between them is not the author: the pack was written by a model that had seen the very corrections a definition
would summarise.

### What was built

| piece | what it does |
|---|---|
| `packages/eval/src/lexicon.ts` | the recipe: a term is a phrase copied from the question (`termOf`), a term is found as words and not as a substring (`occursIn`), a definition is stored only if its term is in the question that taught it (`admitLexicon`), rendered only if the held-out question still contains it (`lexiconPackOf`), and every rendered line is re-read against that question (`licensedLines`, whose reader is now one exported `termOfLine` rather than a regex in two places) |
| `distill-prompt/3` + form `lexicon` | a fourth form beside lesson, repair and procedure: one candidate, `payload.term` copied character for character, statement says what the term denotes, no query inside it |
| arm `full-lexicon` | a second store over the same corrections, rendered under a heading that says what the block is, at the same 1,200-character budget, in the same position |
| `V64-lexicon-is-licensed` | blocking: entries > 0, lines > 0, every rendered term readable, zero unlicensed — three ways to publish a clean null without measuring anything, and the gate refuses all three |
| `V65-lexicon-is-feasible` | advisory, and the one that decides this round: the registration fixed a 25% reach in advance, and a reach of 8.6% makes the round inconclusive by feasibility rather than a refutation |

### What the arm read

**The grain is licensed and almost never renderable.** 179 entries were distilled from 547 corrections — **0.33
per correction** — and those 179 carried **13 distinct terms** a held-out question repeats, so the block rendered
on **132 of 1,534 questions (8.6%)**. Two terms account for 107 of the 132: `cards` (87) and `drivers` (20).

| # | registered prediction | reading |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | the block renders on ≥ 25% of the split | **132 of 1,534 (8.6%)** — refuted, and the first refutation clause fires |
| P2 | beats no memory, clustered | **+0.13pp [−0.59, +0.85]**, 17 gained / 15 lost — not met |
| P3 | beats the rule grain by ≥ 1.0pp | **−0.59pp [−2.09, +0.91]**, 65 / 74 — not met |
| P4 | exchange rate ≥ 1.335 | **0.854** across the split (17/15 on a hurdle of 1.328); on the 132 questions it reached, 5 repairs against 4 breaks, clearance **1.176** — not met on the reading the file fixed |
| P5 | every shown term occurs in its question | **132 of 132 lines licensed**, 0 unlicensed, and the only refusals were 12 candidates with no term at all (`lexicon-no-term`), never a term the question lacked — **holds** |
| P6 | cost within ±20% of `full` | 12 characters against 1,062 — 1.1%, so not met by construction |

**The reason is arithmetic, and it is about the corpus rather than the distiller.** A definition is reusable only
where the corpus reuses a phrase. 179 entries met 13 repeated terms, and 127 of the 132 covered questions already
carried a curated definition from the benchmark itself, so the learned entry was a second copy of a hint the model
already had. The two numbers that bound a second round are the distiller's yield (0.33 entries per correction,
movable by learning from every correction rather than 280 sampled questions) and the corpus's phrase reuse (13
terms from 179 entries, not movable by anything this project can do, because the questions are written
independently and share no terms by design).

**And the published readings now separate two exchange rates, because one arm has two denominators.** Across the
split, 17 repairs against 15 breaks on a hurdle of 1.328 is the reading comparable to R21's bar and to R36's two
rule arms; on the 132 questions the block actually reached, 5 against 4 on a hurdle of 1.063 is the only place a
*rate* is about the grain rather than about the arm's coverage. Both are committed, and `pnpm eval:lexicon`
recomputes them from the artefact with no model call — 17 assertions in CI.

### Four defects, three caught before the push and one by the repository's own check

**The reading was named after a subset and computed over the whole split.** `poc-lexicon.json`'s `onCovered`
field read 17 repaired and 15 broken — the entire 1,534 — while the sentence beside it said "on the questions it
reached" and the CI assertion, written first, said 5 and 4. The field was a copy of the split reading with a name
that promised a filter. Fixed by making the row set the argument: two readings, `exchange.split` and
`exchange.covered`, computed by the same function over different rows, and an assertion that pins each.

**A second `exchangeOf` was written into `lexicon.ts` when `admission.ts` already had one.** The duplicate passed
muster in isolation and was caught by `tsc` as a duplicate identifier at the package boundary — the only place it
could be caught, since a bin is excluded from coverage. Deleted rather than renamed: the arithmetic was identical,
so the honest fix was to call the tested one, and the two-readings property is now asserted on it in
`admission.test.ts`.

**The CI step's independent licence re-check could not run at all.** It built a `RegExp` from a string containing
`\p{L}` and `\$&` inside a shell double-quoted `node -e`, so bash consumed one level of backslash and node
received `[\]\]` and a raw `$&` — a `SyntaxError`, not a failing assertion. This is the step that was supposed to
*not trust the gate*, and it would have failed the build on a green artefact. Replaced with a token match
(`split(/[^a-z0-9]+/)` plus an optional plural), which needs no escaping at all; the step then reported 14 checks.

**The ledger's family count moved and two assertions still said 17.** Adding R37's artefact made the pack-size
family 18 of 18 with 6 positive, and the ledger gate's own criteria ("at least fifteen") still pass, so the
artefact was right and the *assertion* was stale — `a.family.datasets === 17` and a statement containing "12 of the
17". Both are rewritten, and the round is a reminder that a gate on a count is a gate that has to be re-read every
time the set it counts grows (`AUDIT` §34.9).

### What it changes about the product statement

The product line closes on nothing shipping, and that sentence does not change. What changes is the *kind* of
nothing: this is not "a distilled memory does not pay" and not "a definition is the wrong object". It is **a
distilled memory pays only where the same words come back**, and on a corpus of independently written questions
they do not: 8.6% reach against a 25% floor fixed before the run. The grain joins the six closed routes, and the
seventh closure is the first one that is about the corpus rather than about the mechanism.

Sealed by 2,658 tests across 129 files (35 in `lexicon.test.ts`, of which 5 are new for the shared line reader),
four coverage dimensions at **99.98 / 99.67 / 100 / 99.98** with `lexicon.ts` at **100% on all four**, and two
gates (`V64` blocking, `V65` advisory).

## 154 — The ceiling was real, and the reason was wrong

**R38 bought no dispatch and corrected the round before it.** §153 closed the grain route with a number
(8.6% reach) and a cause — "a definition is reusable only where a corpus reuses a phrase, and this one does
not". The number stands. The cause does not, and the correction moves the closure from an assertion about a
distiller to a property of how questions are written.

### Why a zero-call round was the right instrument

The corpus ships a store of definitions of its own, and the record had never read it as one. BIRD attaches
an `evidence` block to **1,386 of 1,534 dev questions (90.35%)**, and the block is a mapping rather than
prose:

```
  Eligible free rate for K-12 = `Free Meal Count (K-12)` / `Enrollment (K-12)`
  driver reference name refers to driverRef
  the label means the class of the molecule
```

Read as `{key, value}` pairs, those annotations *are* the key universe a definitional memory could have had.
So the question that decides whether the route is closed — was 8.6% the corpus's ceiling or the store's
construction? — is answered by ranking the corpus's own keys by the questions they reach. Three narrow
shapes read **1,266 of the 1,386** annotated questions (91.3%), yielding **1,559 distinct keys**, 346 of
which recur in more than one question.

### The first frontier was a frontier of English, and the reading says so

Ranked raw, **two keys reach a quarter of the split**: `list` and `name`. Both are annotated exactly once in
1,534 questions and both occur in hundreds of them. They are not terms the corpus defines — they are words
it happened to write a line about, and a frontier built from them measures the frequency of English.

The separator is the corpus's own judgement rather than a stopword list: **density**, how often a key is
annotated over how often its questions mention it. `single bond` is annotated every time it appears (1.0);
`list` is annotated once in 272 (0.004). And the density structure is the round's finding:

| keys by the number of questions that mention them | mean density |
|---|---|
| three or fewer | **0.967** |
| fifty or more | **0.077** |

**The corpus defines what it mentions once and mentions without defining what it mentions often.** That is
the inversion a definitional store cannot survive, and it explains the whole record without appealing to the
distiller: a memory retrieved by the question's own words can only act on words that come back, and the
corpus withholds its definitions from exactly those.

| store size | raw keys | density ≥ 0.5 | density ≥ 0.8 | density = 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 keys — the arm's own count | 1,026¹ | **241** | 148 | 78 |
| keys to reach 25% | 2 | 53 | 233 | 318 |
| ceiling, every key held | 95.2% | **65.9%** | 55.2% | 52.3% |

¹ not a vocabulary frontier: at 13 keys the raw ranking is still generic words.

### What it does and does not overturn

**It does not overturn the closure.** Holding every key the annotations treat as vocabulary still leaves
**34.1%** of the split unreached at density 0.5 and **47.7%** at density 1.0. No store of definable terms
can render on half of this corpus.

**It does overturn the reason, in the direction that flatters the arm.** At its own 13 terms the vocabulary
frontier is **241 questions** against the arm's licensed **132** — a factor of 1.83, inside the band the
three thresholds produce (241 / 148 / 78). The store was therefore not badly constructed: it was near the
frontier of what 13 keys can do, and the frontier is low. §153's sentence "the distiller's term selection is
far from the frontier" would have been wrong; the honest statement is that **the arm was on the frontier and
the frontier is inside the corpus's own vocabulary**.

| # | registered prediction | reading |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | the raw set crosses 25% within five keys, all generic | **2 keys**, `list` and `name`, densities 0.004 | holds |
| P2 | the vocabulary frontier at 13 keys is under 2× the arm | **241 against 132**, ratio 1.83 | holds |
| P3 | the ceiling at density 0.5 is at most 75% | **65.9%** with all 1,070 keys held | holds |
| P4 | at least two entries per distinct term | **179 entries on 13 terms**, 13.77 | holds |
| P5 | rare keys are annotated more thoroughly than common ones | 0.967 at ≤3 questions against 0.077 at ≥50 | holds |
| P6 | the licence and the renderer agree | **132 licensed, 132 served** | holds |

### Three defects, all in the reading, all caught by the reading disagreeing with itself

**The first frontier was reached in two English words.** Found by looking at what the top keys were, not by
looking at the number: 2 keys reaching 25% is either a discovery or a parser artefact, and it was the second.
Fixed by density — a statistic the corpus already carried.

**The arm's store was scoped by fold only, then by nothing at all.** Scoped by fold it licensed 141 questions
and served 132, which reads as nine questions silently dropped by the character budget. Scoped by nothing it
licensed 201, which reads as a third of the reach lost. The lane scopes its lexicon by fold **and** database
(`lexiconByDomain.get(row.db_id)`); scoped correctly it is **132 licensed, 132 served**, and P6 asserts that.
Both wrong versions were caught the same way — two columns of the same artefact disagreeing — which is why the
reading publishes `armLicensed` beside `renderedQuestions` (`AUDIT` §34.10).

**A refutation clause nobody measured.** The registration's second clause said a key universe covering under
half of the annotations would be the parser's rather than the corpus's, and no column measured it. A clause
that cannot fire is not a clause; `V68-the-annotations-were-parsed` now computes it (1,266 of 1,386, 91.3%)
and blocks below a half.

### Where this leaves the record

The seventh closure stands and is now stated as a property of corpora rather than of mechanisms: **a
definition is reusable only where a corpus repeats the words it defines, and this corpus repeats the words it
leaves undefined.** What a reader can carry to another project is the instrument rather than the verdict —
the frontier curve, the density separator, and the two-column agreement check — all of which cost zero model
calls and apply to any store with keys.

Sealed by **2,689 tests across 130 files**, four coverage dimensions at **99.98 / 99.67 / 100 / 99.98** with
`frontier.ts` at **100% on all four**, three gates (`V66` and `V68` blocking, `V67` advisory), and sixteen
arithmetic assertions in CI over a recomputed artefact.

## 155 — The range was the instrument

**§25.7 has carried the same open item since R30, and it carried it as a schema question:** `eval:power` audits
whole-artefact deltas, an arm inside an artefact is not a row, so the record's arms had to be looked up by hand
and any artefact carrying several arms understated its own positives. *Is an arm an artefact?* was the question
that blocked the fix.

**The answer is no, and an arm does not need to be one.** An artefact is the unit the validity gates certify —
one dataset, one fold partition, one call budget, one set of vetted outcomes. An arm is a column of that same
run. It inherits every gate and contributes one number the gates never read: how many questions changed hands
between it and its control. So the missing thing was never a schema. It was three columns of arithmetic over
`(helped, harmed, n)`.

**What the ledger contains.** 98 arm rows over 20 artefacts, from `arms[]` (control `none`) and `arm_pairs[]`
(control `full`): the delta recomputed from its discordant counts, the 95% half-width, the difference the same
sample could detect at 80% power, whether the delta clears that floor, and — for every row that does not — how
many questions it would take to decide an effect of the size it found. Plus each contrast name across the runs
that measured it, and, for each contrast measured at more than one size, whether its median magnitude fell.

| # | Prediction | Reading | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | fewer than a third of the rows are decided | **18 of 98 — 18.4%**, 27 clear a 95% interval | holds |
| P2 | no decided row is smaller than 4pp | smallest decided row is **4.57pp** | holds |
| P3 | `full − none` measured ≥ 15 times, ≤ 2 decided | **20 runs, 1 decided**, 6 inside a 95% interval | holds |
| P4 | the 1,534 median is under a quarter of the 350 median | **2.86pp → 0.33pp**, ratio 0.11 | holds |
| P5 | at least 15 of 20 are negative | **18 negative, 2 positive** | holds |
| P6 | one price exceeds the corpus by an order of magnitude | **1,457,294 questions** for a −0.07pp row | holds |

**The record's most-quoted number was a design artefact, and the arithmetic says so.** The three sample sizes
impose median floors of **4.38pp at 350 questions, 2.07pp at 1,534 and 0.82pp at 7,000**. The pilots that
produced most of this page's beliefs could not have seen a 1pp effect had one been there, and every row that
*was* decided is larger than 4.5pp. `full − none` — the memory contrast, twenty runs of it — is **18 negatives
and 2 positives, one decided, six inside a 95% interval**, with a median magnitude that falls from **2.86pp on
350 questions to 0.33pp on 1,534**. That is the signature of an exaggerated pilot, not of a mechanism whose
sign wanders.

**The counter-example is why the instrument can be trusted.** `linked`, the schema-pruning channel, reads
**7.71pp at 350 questions and 9.26pp at 1,534**: the only contrast in the record whose effect *grows* with the
sample, decided at both sizes. A rounding artefact does not grow with n. So the ledger separates the one large
effect this project actually measured from the twenty small ones it has been arguing about — and it does so
with the same arithmetic, which is the point.

**Two defects, both found by two columns of the same reading disagreeing.** The first: `values` is **two
contrasts**, +1.17pp against the no-memory baseline and +0.85pp against the `full` arm, and any sentence that
quoted one number for "the channel" was quoting a treatment effect while describing a control comparison. Every
row now carries its `control`, in the row and in the contrast name. The second: the first replication table
called a single decided run a replication, because with one decided row "the decided runs agree" is vacuously
true; `decidedAgree` is `null` below two. Both are `AUDIT` §34.9's defect — a correct computation about the
wrong population — in a new place, and both were caught the way that one was: by a column contradicting another
column rather than by a reviewer.

**What this changes about the two hundred paragraphs above it.** Nothing in them is withdrawn: the numbers are
the numbers, and every one of them reconciles to its own discordant counts. What changes is their standing. Of
the arms this record has quoted — `values` +1.17pp, `full-one` −0.20pp, `full-lexicon` −0.59pp, `full-accepted`
+0.52pp — **not one is decided by its own sample**, and each now appears beside a price: 352 questions for the
cheapest, 1,457,294 for the dearest. A question that costs a million questions is not a question this project
can ask, and writing that down is the difference between a null and an excuse.

Sealed by **2,738 tests across 131 files**, four coverage dimensions at **99.98 / 99.67 / 100 / 99.98** with
`resolution.ts` at **100% on all four**, three gates (`V69` and `V70` blocking, `V71` advisory), and fifteen
arithmetic assertions in CI over a recomputed artefact.

## 156 — The scenario is a package, and the layer table stops being a paragraph

**`AUDIT` §24.7 carried R27's stage 3 as "mechanical and open" since R27 stage 2 closed.** It is now
closed, and the thing that made it worth a section is not the move. Since the first iteration this
project has claimed that the measurement apparatus is scenario-agnostic and that `core` contains no
text-to-SQL. That claim was measured once, by hand, in §136 — 11,764 lines, 37.2% of the repository,
zero in `core` — and never recomputed, which is the shape of every number that quietly stops being true.

**The move.** Six SQL modules and one extracted function became `@agentix-e/microglia-sql`:
`sql-exec`, `sql-guard`, `sql-diff`, `schema-link`, `m-schema`, `value-samples`, plus `canonicalRows`,
which had been hiding inside `sota.ts` and defining what "the same rows" means. The cut is one question
about a signature — *does the function mention a database?* — and the graph it completes is
`core ← protocol ← sql ← eval`, with `browser` beside `eval` and `node` above `browser`.

**Three modules answer yes and stayed, and each has a dependency rather than a shrug.** `bird-data`
opens SQLite to read a *corpus*, and depends on the artefact schema, which is the protocol's.
`link-bind` needs the rule-template engine, which is a knowledge representation. `exec-signature` is a
measurement signal read by the pool. "Mentions SQL" is not the test; *which layer the module depends on*
is.

**The table became a reading.** `pnpm eval:coupling` walks every production module, counts lines,
counts scenario words in **code** (comments stripped by a lexer), reads the package import graph, and
assigns a verdict: `adapter`, `deferred` with a written reason, or `general`.

| layer | modules | lines | coupled modules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core` | 37 | 6,821 | **0** |
| `protocol` | 2 | 1,215 | **0** |
| `sql` | 7 | **1,766** | 5 |
| `eval` | 76 | 24,799 | 12, each with a reason |
| `browser` | 2 | 280 | 0 |
| `node` | 6 | 1,282 | 0 |

**Three gates, all blocking.** `V72` fails when a module outside the adapter carries a scenario word
with no written reason — and also when the walker emits fewer rows than it scanned, because a short
table looks exactly like a complete one. `V73` fails on any package import that points at an equal or
higher layer; five edges exist and every one is downward. `V74` certifies the README's sentence: 37 core
modules, zero scenario words in code, every occurrence inside a test where a scope string is free text.

**Two defects were found, and neither was in the move.** The first: the comment stripper tracked quotes
but not regular expressions, so `/^- "([^"]+)":/` in `lexicon.ts` put it inside a string it never left,
swallowing the module's remaining comments and reporting the module as SQL-coupled — a false positive
that would have been read as a real coupling forever. The second is a product defect the move exposed by
changing nothing: under full-suite load `sql-guard`'s queued-statement test failed intermittently because
**the deadline timer started before the child had finished loading `node:sqlite`**, so 40–80 ms of
instrument overhead could consume a 250 ms deadline and report an answer as a timeout. The child now
