`sample-10-exec` is 1.14pp *below* the first draw. The registered instruction is to stop buying draws
and vary **what the draw is asked**, which is R71.

**The replication check held, which is what makes the delta readable**: `first` 51.71 vs R67's 50.86,
ceiling 59.14 vs 59.71, `exec` 50.86 vs 52.00 — the day moved by under a point.

**Two fixes, both at the level the failure lived at.** `ceilingAmong(verdicts, width)` reads the best
of *the arm's own* first n draws, so two ceilings are two readings of one pool (four tests, one of
which is the exact failure: a right answer at draw 7 must be invisible to a five-draw ceiling).
`V77-every-requested-arm-is-a-row` is blocking and appended last so it reads the final table. R69's
own artefact would fail it now.

**And the module R71 needs.** `content-signal.ts` scores a candidate by what it *says* — does the
result name something the question names, does the query carry a literal the question carries — on
the same question-clustered interval the shape signals get, which required extracting `aucReading`
out of `signalReading` rather than copying the bootstrap. With `sql` and `columns` now recorded per
candidate, R71's first stage costs no model calls: it is arithmetic over a pool that has already been
bought.

**A denominator lesson, recorded because it has now bitten twice.** The signal gate found three
survivors by Holm on this pool (`empty` 0.545, `column-shape` 0.556, `value-type` 0.562) and a
composite worth +2.9pp — over the 138 questions where at least two distinct results existed. The arm
built from that composite scored 1.14pp *below* the first draw over all 350. Both numbers are true;
the record had been quoting the first kind beside results of the second kind.

Gate state: 3,890 tests over 188 files, four coverage dimensions at **100%**, `pnpm check` green,
coupling ledger 177 modules / 20 deferred / `core` 0.

### 173.12 Memory's sign follows one unrecorded number, and dev cannot resolve it

The standing question — *is our memory wrong, or is the way we use it wrong* — got its first
quantitative answer this iteration, from an artefact that was already paid for. R66's dev run records,
per question, the rules that were injected and whether the answer with memory was right where the
answer without it was not. Splitting the 1,534 questions by **how much of the question's own
vocabulary the pack accounts for**:

| tercile of overlap | mean overlap | n | net flips | per 100 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| low | 0.168 | 511 | **−13** | **−2.54** |
| middle | 0.304 | 511 | +2 | +0.39 |
| high | 0.485 | 512 | **+9** | **+1.76** |

Monotone, and it changes sign. Memory is not null; memory is **two regimes averaged into a null**, and
the axis that separates them is lexical overlap between the pack and the question.

**The lane's own signal does not find it.** `coverage` — the field built to describe how much of a
question a rule reaches — has nine points of spread with no direction across its range: −1.72 per 100
at coverage 0 (n = 58), +3.85 at 0.2 (n = 130), −4.67 at 0.333 (n = 150), +12.96 at 0.4 (n = 54). The
number that predicts the sign is the one nobody was recording.

**Both limits, before anything is built on it.** The contrast is **+2.34pp with a bootstrap interval of
[−1.81, +6.46]** — it crosses zero, because 1,534 questions carry 33 discordant flips in total. And a
threshold chosen from these labels is in-sample; cross-fitted it is stable (**0.32–0.43 on all five
folds**) and worth **+5 flips against always-injecting's −2** — +0.46pp, inside its own noise.

So **R72** registers the experiment rather than the reading: two arms on `train` (7,829 questions,
out-of-sample for every published dev cell), because a 4pp tercile contrast needs about **6,000
questions** to resolve at 80% power and dev is short by a factor of four. Its first branch —
"overlap is the axis" — would make routing the lane's default and put every later memory mechanism on
a gated regime instead of a mixture of two.

### 173.13 Heat buys entropy, and a free reader reads nothing

Two registrations closed this iteration and one defect that had been hiding inside a gate got fixed at
the level it lived at. Both readings came from a dispatch that cost **$0.2380** for 2,953 calls — a
third of R66's bill for a quarter of its calls per question, which is what three dispatches outside the
double-priced window now look like.

**R70: temperature is not the lever.** At T = 1.0 against R69's 0.7, on the same 350 questions, the
five-draw ceiling moved **+1.71pp** and the first draw **−0.85pp**. That lands on the registered
`Otherwise` branch — under 5pp of ceiling without a baseline loss — so heat bought no pool and cost no
baseline, and the temperature line is closed.

**The number that decided it is not in the arm table.** Five draws hold **1.446 distinct answers per
question at 0.7** and **1.620 at 1.0**: 234 questions collapsed to a single result at the lower
temperature, 205 at the higher. Heat did what it is supposed to do — 29 more questions got a genuinely
plural pool — and the ceiling gained **6 questions**. Twenty-nine plural pools converted into six
ceilings (21%); the other four fifths of the new entropy is additional *wrong* answers, which is what a
hotter distribution is. Diversity was necessary and nearly inert.

**Voting and shape-selection are the same selector here.** `sample-5 − sample-5-first` is **+2.29pp**
[0.00, 4.57] with 13 gained and 5 lost; `sample-5-exec − sample-5-first` is the same **+2.29pp** with
19 and 11; and `sample-5 − sample-5-exec` is **0.00pp with 16 flips in each direction**. The
registration predicted the first and expected the second to stay at chance, so its numbers held and its
expectation did not — which is the more useful half.

**R71: reading a candidate's content is as inert as reading its shape.** Over R70's pool, zero calls:
`column-mention` **AUC 0.514** [0.458, 0.571], `literal-match` **0.509** [0.500, 0.524],
`content-mean` 0.523, against the baseline draw order 0.509 and the shape family's best of 0.595. The
best top-pick gain on the eligible population is **+0.7pp** against a registered bar of +4pp. Branch:
**content is not free**.

**The narrow interval was the finding.** `literal-match`'s interval is 0.024 wide — the narrowest of the
eight signals this lane has priced — and it is not precision. The signal is constant across the draws
on **342 of 350 questions** (967 candidates at exactly 0, 658 at exactly 1, **8 questions with any
variation**), so the question-clustered bootstrap resamples the same number five times. A width of
0.024 over 1,750 candidates is a statement about how few comparisons exist, not about how well anything
is known. `column-mention` is the same shape less extremely: 783 candidates at exactly 0, variation on
107 of 350. Third time this record has found a number true of its own denominator and false of the run,
and the first time the interval width itself was the tell.

**The defect: a gate written against a list instead of against the table.** `V77` refused R70 — a
complete run of four bought arms, every other gate green — with the message "missing none of 6 bought
arm(s)". `none` is not a row; it is the baseline every row is a delta against. The gate is now
`armCoverageGate` with six tests, `armCoverageOf` replays it against a file, and `pnpm eval:arm-coverage`
walks the repository: **21 artefacts, 62 bought arms, every row present**. The run was deliberately not
re-bought — a re-dispatch draws new samples, so it buys a different measurement rather than a verdict on
the old one — and the replay is a step of `pnpm check` from now on, which turns "did the lane publish
what it paid for" into a property of the repository instead of a property of a run that has already
ended.

**R73 is registered, and it is cheap for an unusual reason.** R71's branch says the next thing to price
is the *written* reader — CHESS's assertions, authored once per question by a model and then executed
per candidate by code. One call per question, 350 calls, **$0.03**, over a pool that already exists.

**R72 was amended before dispatch, and the amendment deleted an arm.** The estimator the registration
was built on now exists as code, and re-deriving it from R66's artefact reproduced the tercile means to
three decimals (0.165 / 0.303 / 0.484) and the whole-population net to the digit (−2, −0.13 per 100) —
while moving two things: the middle tercile is **−3** rather than +2, so the sign change is between
*middle and high*; and the cross-fitted threshold region is **0.38–0.41** rather than 0.32–0.43, which
puts the frozen 0.34 outside it and puts the withheld share at the optimum at **71.8%**, 1.8 points
outside the registration's own 30–70% instrument band. The band gives way, in the open, with the
withheld share reported at every threshold and void reserved for a degenerate gate.

**And `full-overlap` no longer needs to exist.** A rule that chooses between `none` and `full` per
question is *evaluated exactly*, not estimated, from a run that measures both: every question has both
actions observed, so the counterfactual for any deterministic rule over the recorded pack text is
already in the file. Support is full, so this is off-policy evaluation without the approximation. The
dispatch drops from three arms to two — `none` and `full`, `train`, 7,829 questions, ≈18,500 calls,
≈2.7 hours, ≈$1.5 — and the policy is read afterwards for nothing.

**The trap the committed estimator avoids, recorded because it flips the sign.** Rebuilding the pack
from `packIdList` and the item store instead of reading `injected` gives **+0 / +5 / −7** flips — the
opposite gradient — because a store item's `statement` is that item's content in whichever fold wrote
the snapshot, not the text injected under that id.

Gate state: **3,912 tests over 189 files**, four coverage dimensions at **100%**, `pnpm check` green,
coupling ledger **178 modules / 20 deferred / `core` 0**. R72 is in flight on `train`
(≈2.7 hours). R68's second-backbone dispatch never got a runner — it sat `in_progress` for an hour with
no update after the setup step — and was cancelled rather than left holding the concurrency group; it is
re-dispatched once R72 clears.

### 173.14 A gate written over an empty list agrees with everything, and the fallback behind it was unreachable twice

R72 was dispatched three times before it started measuring anything. The three failures are one
defect with three layers, and the run that finally went out is the first two-arm `train` dispatch this
project has priced.

**Layer one: the gate.** `V77`'s sibling — the arm check — asked whether every arm a registration
*declares* had been bought. R72's header declares `arms: full`, and the two baselines are dropped from
both sides, so the declared list is empty, and "every element of the empty set is bought" is true for
any dispatch at all. A dispatch of `gated,oracle` — the R67 ladder — passed the check written to catch
exactly that, measured two planted arms the file never names on 1,566 questions, and stopped only when
the budget forecast added up the remaining folds: **7,235 calls, $0.58, 21 minutes**.

**Layer two: the correction, and the default that made it unreachable.** The rule is now equality in
both directions and reports `unbought` and `undeclared` separately, because "the dispatch buys an arm
the file never names" and "the file names an arm the dispatch does not buy" are different facts that
need different sentences. It was not enough. The dispatch had been sent with an empty `arms` field, the
workflow fell back to a literal `gated,oracle`, and the fallback was **the third representation of one
fact** — worse, the input carried `default: 'gated,oracle'`, so GitHub substituted the default when the
field was empty and the `||` fallback never ran at all. The second dispatch died in 90 seconds on the
corrected check, which is the check earning its keep rather than the check being the plan.

**Layer three: the default is the registration.** `SOTA_ARMS` now falls back to
`steps.registration.outputs.value`, produced by `pnpm eval:prereg-arms --csv prereg/<id>.md` — the same
pattern the sampling temperature already used, for the same reason. An empty header resolves to "the
two baselines" rather than to somebody else's ladder, and the input's default is gone.

**What the void run bought, at $0.58.** The first measurement of a two-arm `train` dispatch:

| per fold (1,566 questions) | calls | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| answering, two arms | 6,264 | **two** calls per question-arm, not one |
| distillation, `learn_sample` 700 | 711 | warm cache |
| adjudication | 260 | |
| fold total | 7,235 | 21 minutes |
| five folds | **39,069** | $3.15 off-peak |

The estimate in R72's amendment was $1.5 and it was wrong by a factor of two for one reason: answering
costs a generation call **and** a repair call, and only the fold totals showed it. The re-dispatch went
out at cap 44,000, deadline 175 minutes.

**R73 is implemented, and the writer is one call per question.** CHESS's selection step is a *writer*:
assertions authored for this question against these results, executed per candidate. R71 priced the
free approximation and found it inert — the signals were not weak, they were not per-question facts.
`assertion.ts` is the other half, and it is all arithmetic:

- the grammar is three executable kinds — `column:<name>`, `value:<literal>`, `rows:<n>` — and nothing
  else, because a comparison operator is a second grammar and a disjunction a third, and a writer that
  can say anything can say something no arithmetic can refute;
- three assertions per kind, which is the registration made binding: the scorer counts satisfied
  assertions, so a writer that emitted twenty sentences would outvote one that emitted three without
  being more informative;
- the parser is tolerant of prose and intolerant of a malformed count — `rows:several` is dropped
  rather than read as zero, because zero is an assertion the writer never made;
- the reading reports `assertion-column`, `assertion-value`, `assertion-rows` and their sum on the same
  question-clustered axis as every other selector, because the arm is a claim about *which sentence*
  carries the ranking and a combined number alone could not say that.

The writer runs in the lane, one call per question, and its reply lands in the same `per_case` entry as
the candidates it scores — so `pnpm eval:assertion` re-derives the reading from the artefact with zero
calls. `SOTA_ASSERTION_CACHE` keys a reply on the full prompt, so a replay of the same split pays
nothing for the assertions and measures the same ones.

**A gate that was missing, found while declaring the arm.** R73's header named `sample-5-assert` before
the arm existed, and nothing noticed until `parseArms` would have refused it at dispatch — R67 lost a
dispatch exactly that way, to `sample-5-exec`. `pnpm eval:prereg` now refuses any header naming a
`sample-` arm the lane cannot buy. The restriction to that prefix is deliberate: the header is read by
three vocabularies (this lane's `sample-N-selector` family, tau-bench's `memory`/`reference`, and the
retired BIRD arms), and "every arm must exist" would refuse files that are correct.

### 173.15 The negative effect has a coordinate, and its whole domain is negative

R72 landed on `train`: 7,829 questions, five folds, two arms, **16,876 calls, $1.4039, 78.1% cache
hit**. The headline is the third independent population on which the prefix pack is negative, and the
first one narrow enough to exclude zero:

| reading | without | with | delta | 95% CI | p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| whole split, 7,829 | 56.57% | 55.73% | **−0.84pp** | [−1.44, −0.26] | 0.0054 |

**The routing table is the finding, and it is monotone.**

| tercile | mean overlap | n | injecting (95% CI, p) | gate gain at 0.30 (95% CI, p) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| low | 0.081 | 2,609 | **−1.46pp [−2.45, −0.50], p 0.0042** | **+2.91pp [1.00, 4.91], p 0.0042** |
| middle | 0.197 | 2,609 | −0.69pp [−1.69, 0.31], p 0.1973 | +1.38pp [−0.61, 3.37] |
| high | 0.355 | 2,611 | −0.38pp [−1.49, 0.69], p 0.5287 | +0.61pp [−0.61, 1.84] |

The registered branch fires — *overlap is the axis*, +2.91pp with an interval that excludes zero — and
three things have to travel with it, because the branch sentence alone would be read as a win.

**One: the sign never turns positive.** The registered expectation was "low overlap hurts, high overlap
helps"; what replicates is "below-median overlap hurts and the top two thirds are a wash". Only the low
tercile's interval excludes zero.

**Two: "high overlap" here means "less unrelated", not "on topic".** Every tercile mean sits below 0.5 —
0.081, 0.197, 0.355 — because a pack of a few dozen rules does not repeat half of a question's
vocabulary. So overlap measures **how much damage a pack does** and never measures gain.

**Three: the gate's benefit is entirely the absence of harm, and against injecting nothing it is zero.**
At 0.30 the routed policy scores 56.55% against `none`'s 56.57% — **−0.02pp**. At the in-band 0.20 it
scores 56.35%, **−0.22pp**. Every positive number in the policy column is measured against
always-injecting, which is the worse arm. A gate that withholds 77% of its packs and lands one hundredth
of a point below "do not inject" has not made memory useful; it has made memory **free**.

Both statements are true and only one is a result: the pack is not harmful when it shares the question's
vocabulary, and it is not helpful when it does. The prefix position is closed as a **source of accuracy**
— not as a mechanism subject of study.

`pnpm eval:overlap` gained `tercileVerdicts`, so the three readings are recomputable from any artefact:
injecting, routing and gate gain per tercile, each with the McNemar interval the branch condition names
and the tercile table alone could not supply.

### 173.16 Reading is bounded by the pool, and the pool is one third the size it was registered at

R73 landed on `minidev` in 24 minutes: **3,165 calls** against the 5,600 cap that Amendment 2 bought.
350 writer replies, zero failures, all cached.

| arm | accuracy | delta vs none | 95% CI | p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | 52.57% | — | — | — |
| `full` | 53.43% | +0.86pp | [−2.00, 3.71] | 0.7011 |
| `sample-5-first` | 51.14% | −1.43pp | [−4.00, 1.14] | 0.4049 |
| `sample-5-assert` | 52.29% | −0.29pp | [−2.57, 2.00] | 1.0000 |

The arm against its control is **+1.15pp**. Four questions.

| signal | AUC | 95% CI | top pick | eligible |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `assertion-column` | 0.544 | [0.481, 0.604] | 28.70% | 115 |
| `assertion-value` | **0.500** | **[0.500, 0.500]** | 26.09% | 115 |
| `assertion-rows` | 0.562 | [0.494, 0.626] | 26.96% | 115 |
| `assertion-hits` | 0.581 | [0.492, 0.667] | 29.57% | 115 |

Every interval straddles 0.5, so the registered branch is *the writer is not the price*. Three
diagnostics outlive the null:

- **`assertion-value` is exactly 0.500 with a zero-width interval.** The signal does not vary on any of
  the 115 eligible questions: a `value:` assertion names a literal the question states, and all five
  draws of a question either return that literal or none of them do. This is R71's `literal-match`
  phenomenon taken to its limit — R71 varied on 8 of 350, this varies on none of 115. **A reader cannot
  rank candidates on a property the candidates agree about.** Third zero-width interval in this lane,
  third time the width was the tell.
- **The strongest single kind is the one the file pre-dismissed.** The registration expected `column:`
  to carry the claim and called `rows:` a shape signal "this lane already knows is inert". Measured:
  `rows:` 0.562 against `column:` 0.544. The prior was inverted.
- **The ceiling was the population.** The file predicted 205 of 350 questions would collapse to a single
  distinct result; 235 did, so the eligible population is **32.9%** of the split and the detection floor
  is an AUC of about **0.59**. A 115-question population excludes a strong reading and cannot exclude a
  weak one, so the mechanism is underpowered by construction rather than refuted.

### 173.17 What four experiments say together about memory's negative effect

R70 through R73 each closed one candidate explanation, and the four answers stack into a coordinate
system rather than a list.

| experiment | question | answer | size of the effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R70 | does sampling width buy accuracy? | yes, at 21% entropy conversion | +2.29pp from five draws, ceiling +1.71pp over first |
| R71 | can content be read for free? | no, twice on two signal families | AUC 0.514 / 0.509, both straddle 0.5 |
| R72 | is the sign a routing property? | yes, monotone and negative everywhere | −1.46 / −0.69 / −0.38pp by tercile |
| R73 | does a written per-question reader recover it? | not at this population size | 0.581, interval [0.492, 0.667], four questions |

The negative effect is now located on three coordinates, and only one of them has been priced:

- **position** — a pack shown *before* the question. R72 closes it as a source of accuracy: the best
  regime is a wash, and gating reaches the harm but not the benefit.
- **dose** — 1.86 rules per question, 33.2% of injections belonging to a rule whose net contribution is
  negative (267 harmful against 236 helpful rules out of 1,709 ever injected). This is an **observational**
  attribution: a rule's sign is estimated from the questions it happened to be injected on, and rules
  are not injected at random.
- **content** — 2,628 rules built out of 7,829 questions' failures, of which 1,206 are neutral. The
  distillation writes a rule per failure and most failures do not generalise.

The third coordinate is the one the user's own hypothesis points at — that what we memorise and how we
use it are wrong — and it is the only one still measured by a confounded instrument. A rule that is
injected on hard questions and withheld from easy ones looks harmful whatever its content is. **The
next experiment randomises the dose**, which is the one design that turns the observational attribution
into a causal one at a price this lane can pay.

### 173.18 The rule verdict was a selection effect, and one withheld rule per question is the fix

`attribution.ts` reports **267 harmful, 236 helpful, 1,206 neutral** rules of the 1,709 ever injected,
and 33.2% of all injections belong to a harmful rule. Every one of those verdicts is observational: a
rule is scored on the questions that happened to retrieve it, and retrieval is a similarity function
over content, which is a function of topic, which is a function of difficulty. A rule that fires on
hard questions reads as harmful whatever it says, and pruning 267 rules on that evidence would be
acting on a selection effect worth about 4.4pp of the negative if real and nothing if not.

**R74 makes it causal, and it is the first arm in this lane that prices a rule rather than a pack.**

- **The arm.** `loo` renders the pack `full` renders with **exactly one rule removed**, chosen by
  `looIndex(pack.items.length, question + fold)` — a hash of the question's own text. Nothing is
  re-retrieved and nothing is re-cut, so if the cell moves, the withheld rule moved it.
- **The pairing.** Within a question the other rules and the model are held fixed, so `loo − full` is
  attributable to one rule. Across the split a rule is withheld on a random subset of the questions
  that drew it, so a **group** verdict — harmful, helpful, neutral, one-rule packs, three-rule packs —
  is unconfounded.
- **The classes are computed from the same artefact**, by the arithmetic `attribution.ts` uses. One
  file joined to itself is what makes the class reproducible; a reading that needed a second stage's
  output could not be re-derived from the run.
- **The reading is free.** `pnpm eval:loo` prints the whole-split delta, the class table, the pack-size
  table and the draw distribution, with zero calls.
- **`looIndex` returns −1 for an empty pack, not 0.** A question the retriever offered nothing for has
  no rule to withhold; filing it as "dropped the first rule" would put every empty pack in the same
  bucket as the one-rule packs and silently compare two different things.
- **The hash, not a draw.** A `--seed` on a dispatch puts the seed outside the registration, and a rule
  chosen by a number nobody recorded makes "the effect of dropping rule r" a statement about one run
  of one script.

| item | calls | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| answering, three arms | 23,487 | 2 calls per question-arm |
| distillation, `learn_sample` 700 | 711 | R70's rate |
| adjudication, three arms | 390 | |
| **total** | **≈24,600** | **≈$2.0** off-peak, ≈90 minutes |

Dispatch `42856739453`, cap 28,000, deadline 170. The cap is R72's own fold totals scaled to a third
arm rather than a table estimate, because the last three registrations each discovered that the
budget was the moving part.

The four branches are ordered and partition: **void** (under 5,000 pairs, or a withheld share under
60%); **the attribution is causal** (harmful recovers ≥ +1.0pp and helpful loses ≥ 1.0pp, both
excluding zero → prune the 267, the first intervention here that *removes* memory); **the confound is
the whole story** (both extreme classes straddle zero → no per-rule verdict in this project can be
trusted, and the next experiment is R66's position); **the dose is what hurts** (the whole split clears
+0.5pp with no separation between classes → the pack is too large at 1.86 rules and the next
registration is a causal dose curve).

### 173.19 The instrument was mislabelled, and half of every minidev effect was the label

Jin, Choi, Zhu and Kang (*Pervasive Annotation Errors Break Text-to-SQL Benchmarks and Leaderboards*,
PVLDB 19(5):931–944, 2026) put BIRD Mini-Dev's annotation error rate at **52.8%** and showed that
re-scoring sixteen published agents against corrected gold moved relative accuracy by −7% to +31% and
ranks by up to nine places. This repository pinned Mini-Dev at `v1-2024-06-20`, and against the
corrected release **151 of the 350 questions in the transfer slice — 43.1% — have a different gold**.

Every small effect in this lane was measured on that slice. R73's entire finding was "four questions
moved". So the experiments were not re-run — a new sample of the same population carries the same
labels — the **artefacts were re-scored**: `per_case` holds `predictedSql`, `baselineSql` and `dbId`,
so both arms can be re-executed against corrected gold with **zero model calls**.

**Fourteen minidev artefacts, all 350 questions matched in every file.**

| reading | uncorrected labels | corrected labels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mean Δ (memory − no memory) | **−2.72pp** | **−1.33pp** |
| runs with Δ < 0 | 13 of 14 | 11 of 14 |
| runs whose Δ excluded zero | 5 | 2 |
| no-memory baseline | 54.02% | **51.26%** |
| memory arm | 51.14% | 49.81% |

**Branch 2 of R75 fires**: five significant verdicts before, one stable and four `fragile` after, none
reversed. The registered sentence is the finding — *nothing measured on 350 questions may be called a
finding again* — and four things travel with it.

**The direction is robust; the magnitude is not.** Across fourteen dispatches and seven memory
mechanisms (dose, framing, transfer, anchoring, clearance, substrate, repair), **no memory variant has
produced a positive effect on this slice** under either grading. That is the strongest replication the
lane has, and it is a claim about a sign rather than a size.

**The correction costs the baseline more than the memory arm.** 54.02 → 51.26% for no-memory (−2.76pp)
against 51.14 → 49.81% for memory (−1.33pp). **Part of the harm this project measured was the baseline
being graded too kindly** — a finding that belongs to nobody's hypothesis, and the mechanical
explanation is that the corrected gold is often a different question, and a pack built from the
corpus's own failures happens to agree with it slightly more often than a bare prompt does.

**The absolute numbers were inflated by 2.8pp.** 54.02% was not this lane's minidev baseline; **51.26%**
is. Every published minidev cell moves by that much.

**The instrument is now the size of the effect.** One question is 0.286pp at n = 350 and the detection
floor for a paired difference is about 2.5pp; corrected effects are 1.4–3.1pp. Two decisions follow:
**minidev is demoted to a smoke test** and may not carry a finding — the smallest population that may
is dev's 1,534 (0.065pp per question), the preferred one train's 7,829 — and **the corrected labels
become the default grading for minidev**, which is a manifest revision plus a patch overlay, registered
separately because a run before the change is not comparable to one after it.

**R72's −0.84pp on train is untouched**: the corrected release covers mini-dev only, and the 336 id
matches against train are collisions between two id spaces. The out-of-sample split is now the only
population whose effect sizes this lane will quote.

### 173.20 Two defects the reading found in its own instrument

**A null cannot be reversed.** `relabelVerdict` classified a sign flip as `reversed` before checking
whether the original delta had ever excluded zero, so R73's +0.86pp (p = 0.70) becoming −0.57pp
(p = 0.86) was reported as the withdrawal of a published verdict. There was no published verdict. The
classifier now returns `absent`, and R75's branch 3 is read only against deltas that had an interval.

**A reading tool that does not close its pool is indistinguishable from a slow database.**
`BoundedSql` holds child processes; a bin that never closes them finishes its work and then idles at
zero CPU until the step timeout. Three runs were killed that way — each having done two minutes of work
and then waiting forty — before the cause was found. The pool is closed in a `finally` now.

### 173.21 The budget was an estimate wearing a bound's clothes, and R68 paid for it twice

R74's dispatch measured fold 1 at 5,483 calls, projected 29,609, and stopped against a 28,000 cap,
**discarding the fold it had just paid for**. Two defects in two layers:

- **An estimate had a bound's authority.** `forecastBudget` compared the projection against the same
  number the operator wrote as the cap. Only the **ceiling** may end a run now: a projection that
  exceeds the cap but fits the ceiling raises the cap to itself (`LlmClient.authoriseCalls`, upward
  only, non-finite ignored) and says so, and the artefact records `cap`, `ceiling` and `cap_in_force`.
- **The estimate was arithmetic in a Markdown table**, and it was the moving part in four consecutive
  registrations. `pnpm eval:budget` derives it from an artefact: the measured rate, the projection, and
  a ceiling that is a *multiple* rather than a number whenever a requested arm was never measured.

**R68 found the second defect in that tool one level down.** Its projection assumed arms cost alike;
R68's three arms are five-draw sampling arms, so the run was dispatched at 4,179 calls for a run that
needed 5,638. `planBudget` now counts **draws rather than arms** — 350 × 16 draws × the per-draw rate =
4,642 with a 1.3× ceiling of 6,035, which covers the measured need. The measured miss is 18% after
weighting against 35% before, and the multiple is 1.3 because it has to cover the next miss rather than
the last one.

`ceiling_calls` would have been the twenty-sixth `workflow_dispatch` input and GitHub's cap is 25 — the
repository's own workflow checker refused the push. The transfer and density knobs moved to repository
variables; forty registrations had never varied them, and a form field nobody varies spends a slot on a
constant.

Gate state: **4,021 tests over 193 files**, four coverage dimensions at **100%**, `pnpm check` green,
coupling ledger **182 modules / 21 deferred / `core` 0**. R74 is in flight on `train` (three arms,
27,846 forecast / 33,416 ceiling); R68's third attempt is in flight on `zhipu:glm-4.7-flashx` sized
from its own measured fold (5,220 / 6,300, deadline 300).

### 173.22 The attribution was two thirds selection effect, and the residue cannot pay for a pruning

R74 ran on `train`: three arms, **24,465 calls**, 105 minutes, and `config.budget.cap_in_force = 29,587`
against a forecast of 27,846 — **the ceiling fired on its first live run**, which is why this file has
an outcome instead of a second void.

| reading | value |
| --- | --- |
| `full` | 55.66% |
| `loo` (one rule withheld per question) | 55.65% |
| whole-split Δ | **−0.01pp** [−0.52, 0.51], p = 1.0000 |
| withheld rules | 532 distinct, median 10 draws, max 88 |

**The class table says two opposite things depending on where the class was decided.**

| class | in-sample Δ | p | cross-fitted Δ | p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| harmful | **+2.37pp** [1.54, 3.21] | < 0.0001 | **+0.82pp** [−0.08, 1.73] | 0.0978 |
| helpful | **−2.84pp** [−3.84, −1.88] | < 0.0001 | −0.33pp [−1.42, 0.77] | 0.6241 |
| neutral | −0.51pp [−1.38, 0.36] | 0.2888 | −0.43pp [−1.25, 0.37] | 0.3379 |

A rule is called harmful *because* the `full` arm failed on the questions that drew it, and the effect
is then measured on those same questions: **a question that was unlucky is a question whose rules were
labelled harmful, and a second draw on it improves regardless of the rule.** `looCrossFitted` decides
each rule's class on the other four folds and measures on the fifth. **65% of the harmful signal and
88% of the helpful one were the fold that produced the label.**

**What survives.** Only a direction, at p = 0.0978, on the harmful class — the first out-of-sample
evidence this project has that any per-rule quality signal exists. It is not a lever: +0.82pp on the
43% of questions that drew a harmful rule projects to **+0.35pp on the split**, where one question is
0.013pp and a paired interval is ±0.4pp. **The intervention would be indistinguishable from noise**, and
the helpful class has no measured basis at all, so the pruning can only be one-sided.

**The consequence for what memory contains.** The per-rule verdicts this project has been using to
decide what goes into the pack are **two thirds regression artifact**, which is a defect in
`attribution.ts` as a *decision input*. And the residual is too small to act on. So the whole-split null
now has a third explanation that neither the in-sample nor the cross-fitted table can rule out: **most
rules are inert**, and a pack cannot help if most of its rules do nothing.

**The next registration follows from that sentence.** Its question is not "which rules are harmful" but
**"how many of the 540 rules change any answer at all"** — the inert share — measured by randomising
*which* rule is withheld across draws rather than holding one hash draw per question. Registered
separately, because it is a different instrument.

**A defect that had been silent for two iterations.** `pnpm eval:loo` had **never produced output**: the
command was registered in `package.json`, the module had sixteen tests, and the binary exported `main`
without calling it. A script that exits zero and prints nothing — every gate in the repository passed,
and the numbers above only exist because the reading was finally run.

### 173.23 The zero the validator refused was the lane's deterministic form

R77 asks the question R74 left behind — **does a rule change what the model writes at all** — and it can
only be asked at temperature zero: a deterministic decoder given two prompts that differ by one rule
returns the same query if and only if the rule did not matter. The header validator refused that
outright, holding `temperature` to `(0, 2]`, and the reason it gave was right and aimed at the wrong set
of registrations:

> a zero here is a deterministic run wearing a sampling arm's name, and it would be reported as a pool
> of identical draws without saying so.

That is exactly true of a registration declaring `sample-<n>` — five draws at zero are one draw counted
five times. It is not true of one declaring `none` and `loo`, which has one draw and no pool to
degenerate. Applied there, the rule protected nothing and made the lane's ordinary deterministic form
inexpressible; it also made R74's temperature invisible, because a file that says nothing inherits the
workflow's 0.7 and nothing in the artefact records what was inherited. The rule now follows the reason
rather than the number: the interval is `[0, 2]` and zero is refused **only** when a `sample-` arm is
present.

| registration | at T = 0 | before | now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `arms: sample-5-first` | five draws are one draw | refused | refused — `whose draws would all be one draw` |
| `arms: none,loo` | one draw, no pool | refused — `describes no draw` | **accepted** |

**R77's own header was 50% light, in the same way R68's was.** The first version priced it at 4,600
calls for "two arms"; the run buys three, because `none` and `full` are measured on every dispatch
whether or not a header names them, and `loo` is the third. Priced from R74's measured 24,465 calls at
**1.0416 per question per draw** (`pnpm eval:budget`, the draw-weighted planner that replaced
per-arm pricing after R68 under-reported by 18%), 2,000 questions over `none,full,loo` projects to
**6,875**, ceiling **7,600**, ≈$0.60. The correction is the same error class the budget gate was built
for: a projection computed over the arms a file happens to list rather than the arms the run bills.

Dispatched as `42915903394` — `train`, 2,000 questions, `none,full,loo`, `temperature: 0`, forecast
6,875 / ceiling 7,600 / deadline 150. The reading is a **count over `per_case`**, not a model call:
`predictedSql` is the `full` arm's query, `armSql.loo` is the same question with one rule withheld, and
the pair is *live* when the two normalise differently. Three branches: **above 70%** and the pack's
premise is wrong rather than its dose (the next intervention is the distillation prompt); **below 30%**
and most rules are live in the wrong direction (the dose is the only remaining axis); **within 2pp of
R74's 52.0%** and the temperature-0.7 decoder was nearly deterministic on this prompt, so the mixture
was never a mixture.

Gate state: **4,021 tests over 193 files**, four coverage dimensions at 100% (branch 99.87),
`pnpm check` green at `f3aa22c`, coupling ledger 182 modules / 21 deferred / `core` 0. In flight: R77
(6,875 / 7,600) and R68's third attempt on `zhipu:glm-4.7-flashx`.

### 173.24 The relabel population was two populations, and every mini-dev accuracy was 8.7pp too low

R75 re-scored fourteen mini-dev artefacts against the corrected labels and reported a mean effect of
**−2.72pp → −1.33pp**. The corrected file is the `sql_only` configuration of Arcwise-Plat, which by its
own description keeps the questions and replaces only the gold. It keeps *its* questions: **67 of the
350 questions in this slice have different text in it**, because BIRD shipped further Mini-Dev
revisions after the `v1-2024-06-20` this repository pins — its 2026 release realigned the ids to 0–499
and rewrote the questions again. On 44 of the 67 the gold moved too.

So the population is two, and they are different instruments:

| population | n | Δ original | Δ corrected | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| whole slice, as first reported | 350 | −2.71pp | −1.33pp | a mixture |
| **question unchanged** | **283** | **−3.03pp** | **−1.34pp** | a relabelling |
| question rewritten | 67 | ≈0 | ≈0 | a corpus revision |

**The conclusion survives intact and two wrong numbers became visible.**

| reading, on the 283 | pinned labels | corrected labels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| memory arm | 59.67% | 58.30% |
| baseline | **62.69%** | **59.64%** |
| paired Δ | −3.03pp | **−1.34pp** |

The mixture reported **54.02% → 51.26%** for the baseline, so every mini-dev accuracy this lane has
quoted was about **8.7pp too low**: the 67 mis-paired rows score 14.93% and 16.31% and drag both arms
down by seven points. They cancel out of a paired difference — both arms are equally wrong on a question
neither was asked — which is why the *effect* was right and the *level* was wrong. 11 of 14 artefacts
keep their sign on the clean population; the two that land on exactly 0.00pp are nulls becoming null
rather than verdicts being withdrawn.

**The instrument is now a pinned revision rather than a reading.** `eval/manifests/gold/` holds the
corrected labels beside the pinned corpus, with their digest and citation in the manifest, identified
offline by the two null-`evidence` rows its own card names (ids **1507** and **1528**) — a lookalike
built from the `full` configuration shares all 498 ids and would fail that check. `reviseGold` replaces
the labels it can and **drops** the rows it cannot, because grading an answer to question A against
question B's label is a corpus revision wearing a relabelling's name. A dispatch chooses
(`gold: corrected`), and every artefact now records the revision it scored against, how many labels it
replaced, and how many questions it could not score. `vendor` stays the default, so no published cell
moved, and a run that keeps it now says so in a field that did not exist.

### 173.25 R77's first dispatch was authorised for two thirds of itself

`42915903394` ran fold 1 and stopped:

```
[sota] fold 1/5: eval=400 learn=700 ... calls=1952
[sota] budget forecast after fold 1/5: the run needs about 10541 calls, the ceiling is 7600 (short by 2941)
```

1,952 calls, no artefact. **The ceiling did what R74's amendment built it to do** — only a ceiling may
end a run — but it ended a run whose *authorisation* was wrong rather than one whose forecast was.
Nothing was overspent; the run was refused permission to finish.

The projection came from `pnpm eval:budget`, which priced 2,000 questions × 3 arms at R74's measured
**1.0416 calls per question per draw**. That rate is a mixture, and the mixture is the defect: R74's
bill was two costs. Evaluation scales with the population; the learning pass scales with the fold count
and with `learn_sample`, and R74's `GenerationCache` answered **2,624 of its 3,500** learning requests,
so 96% of its rate was marginal. Multiplied onto a fifth of its questions with a cold cache, the cheap
part is priced correctly and 700 calls per fold go unpriced.

**This is the third instance of one error class, and each instance moved up a level.** R64 sized a run
by arm count; R68 found the arm count was a draw count; this one found that a per-question rate is a
rate only over the part of the bill that is per question.

`planBudget` now subtracts the prior's learning from its bill before deriving the rate, prices the
dispatch's learning separately, and splits the two numbers by what they can know: the **projection**
prices learning at the share the prior's cache answered, and the **ceiling** prices it in full plus 20%,
because the first fold of any run has nothing to hit and the share cannot transfer.

| R77 as priced | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rate | 1.0416 | **1.0043** |
| projected | 6,875 | 7,593 |
| ceiling | 6,875 | **11,249** |
| the run's own forecast | 10,541 | 10,541 — now inside the ceiling |

`amortisedLearning` marks the case that produced the error: a dispatch that learns against a prior that
does not say how much of its bill was learning still gets a number, and the number says it is a ratio
over a mixture. Re-dispatched as `42922152605` at 11,000 forecast / 12,000 ceiling / deadline 200.

Gate state: **4,055 tests over 194 files**, coverage 100/99.88/100/100, `pnpm check` green at `717809e`,
coupling ledger **183 modules / 22 deferred / `core` 0**. In flight: R77 second dispatch, R68's third
attempt on `zhipu:glm-4.7-flashx`.

### 173.26 The pair-level inert share is a count at temperature zero, and the tool to read it costs nothing

R74 measured that with one rule withheld, **4,074 of 7,829 questions produced byte-identical SQL** — 52%
— and the number cannot be separated from the temperature it was measured at. At T = 0.7 the same prompt
returns the same query twice by chance, so "unchanged" is a mixture of a rule that did nothing and a
decoder that did not move. At T = 0 it is not a statistic: a deterministic decoder given two prompts
that differ by one rule returns the same query **if and only if** the rule did not matter. R77 buys that
reading; `pnpm eval:inert` reads it from the artefact at zero calls.

Three judgement calls live in the code rather than in a paragraph. A pair whose statement failed to
parse is **not** inert — a rule that breaks the query did something, and counting it as nothing would
report a pack as harmless because it is destructive. Case is **not** folded into the main reading, so
`select 1` and `SELECT 1` count as live and the number of pairs that differ only by case is printed
beside the share. A question nothing was withheld from is excluded, because it says nothing about a rule.

Run on R74's own file, where the tool itself prints that the temperature is not zero:

| reading | value |
| --- | --- |
| pairs compared | 7,822 (7 with no statement on one side, excluded) |
| inert | 4,250 — **54.33%** |
| live pairs that differ only by case | 19 |
| rules ever withheld | 532; draws per rule median 10, p90 34, max 88 |
| **rules that changed no answer on any draw** | **26 — 4.9% of the pack** |
| live share 25–50% / 50–75% / 75–100% | 218 / 178 / 76 rules |
| concentration | the busiest tenth of the rules produced **34.4%** of the live answers |

**Two things follow, and both were predictions R77 registered.** Half the pairs are identical while
almost no rule is wholly inert, which is what a 54% pair-level share and a 5% per-rule inertness look
like together: a rule drawn ten times and live five of them contributes five inert pairs and is not
inert. And the liveness is concentrated — a third of it from a tenth of the pack — which is the shape a
distillation prompt that over-produces would leave. Neither number can be believed at T = 0.7, where
both coincidence and sampling noise are doing the work; both are what R77 exists to settle.

`R76` is registered alongside it: `minidev` on the **283** questions the correction can label, with
`gold: corrected`, 1,015 calls projected and a 2,494 ceiling. Its refutations are all instrument
failures — `n` of 350 means the revision was applied after the pool was drawn, `dropped` of anything but
67 means the manifest and the corpus disagree about which questions those are, a null `dataset_gold`
means the dispatch's choice never reached the loader, and a baseline within 1pp of 51.26% means the
67 mis-paired rows are still in the denominator. It is a validation that is *registered* because an
instrument tested only in pieces is the shape of every silent failure this lane has recorded.

Gate state: **4,071 tests over 195 files**, coverage 100/99.86/100/100, `pnpm check` green at `c6b5d4a`.
In flight: R77 second dispatch (11,000 / 12,000), R68's third attempt on `zhipu:glm-4.7-flashx`.

### 173.27 — The forecast charged the cold fold's learning to four folds that read it from the cache

R77's reading arrived: `42922152605`, **6,946 calls, $0.531**, five folds, 2,000 questions,
`none,full,loo` at temperature 0. It is inside the **7,600** the *first* dispatch was authorised for,
which means the first dispatch was never under-sized — it was stopped by the in-run forecast. Fold 1
cost 1,952 (1,200 evaluation, **700 learning**, 52 other); `forecastBudget` multiplied that fold by five
and reported 10,541 against a 7,600 ceiling. In the completed run the `GenerationCache` answered
**2,623 of 3,500** learning requests, so the entire learning pass cost **877 calls and not 3,500**.

This is the third level of one error class, and each level was found by the layer above failing:

| level | instrument | what it conflated | found by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R64 | `planBudget` | arms with questions | a run 4× over |
| R68 | `planBudget` | arms with draws | a run 2× over |
| R77 Amd 1 | `planBudget` | per-question rate with cache-warm rate | forecast 10,541 for a 6,946 run |
| R77 Amd 2 | `forecastBudget` | a start-up cost with a per-fold price | the same dispatch, actually finishing |

`FoldSpend.learning` now carries the learning calls **measured around the pass** (`llm.stats.calls`
before and after `buildFoldMemory`), not inferred from the question count, and the extrapolation takes
the maximum of `calls - learning` rather than of `calls`. Netting before the maximum rather than after
keeps the original rule — remaining folds are priced at the dearest one — while refusing to charge a
one-off to folds that read it from a cache.

Replayed on both ledgers, with nothing else changed:

| dispatch | forecast then | forecast now | actual | error then | error now | cap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R77 (1,952 after fold 1, 700 learning) | 10,541 | **7,461** | 6,946 | +52% | **+7.4%** | 7,600 — finishes, 139 spare |
| R74 (5,483 after fold 1) | 29,609 | **≤ 26,529** | 24,465 | +21% | ≤ +8.4% | 28,000 — finishes above 366 learning calls |

R74's row is a **threshold, not a replay**: its artefact records calls per fold and not learning per
fold, because the field did not exist. The break-even is 366 calls of learning in fold 1 and the pass
cost 877 in a run built the same way, so the direction is not in doubt and the figure is a bound. The
test carrying it asserts the break-even rather than a measurement the artefact cannot support — the
same discipline that made R75's correction a pinned revision instead of a patched file.

Three tests pin the behaviour (R77 replay, R74 break-even, net-of-maximum when a *later* fold is dearer)
and two pin the edges that make shipping it safe: a fold with no `learning` field forecasts **exactly**
as before, so no published figure moves, and `learning > calls` is clamped rather than subtracted,
because a negative cost would quietly raise the ceiling the run believes it has. `writeStop` now records
`learning_calls` per completed fold so the next partial artefact shows which part of a fold's bill the
remaining folds inherit and which part they get free. **21 tests in `call-budget.test.ts`, 4,076 over
195 files, coverage 100/99.86/100/100, `pnpm check` green.**

What the mistake cost: **1,952 calls, about $0.15**, and one discarded fold. What it bought is the
distinction the lane had been missing since R64 — a run's bill is a per-question part and a one-off
part, and only the first belongs in a rate.

**`R77`'s outcome, recorded in the same file.** 55.73% of pairs are inert at T = 0 (1,114 of 1,999),
**113 rules — 23.9% of the pack — never changed an answer on any draw**, and the busiest tenth produced
33.3% of the live answers. Prediction 1 (30–55%) is falsified by 0.73pp **and in the direction that
matters**: the deterministic share is *above* the mixture it was supposed to be a component of, which
kills the "52% was coincidence" explanation. Prediction 2 was arithmetically impossible as written —
per-rule inertness is an extreme and pair-level inertness an average, so the extreme is *below* the
average unless the pack is bimodal. No branch fired. `none` 61.55% / `full` 61.80% / `loo` 60.90%:
withholding one rule **improves** accuracy by −0.90pp [−1.90, 0.10], p = 0.0886, the widest-sample
out-of-sample negative reading this lane has, and the first at temperature zero. The next measurement
is not a pruning: 113 rules at a median of 3 draws is weak evidence per rule, so those 113 get **more
draws** before anything is deleted.

### 173.28 — The correction reached the scorer, and the level it predicted was right to 0.28pp

R76 ran end to end: `42931789908`, **910 calls** against 1,015 projected, five folds, 283 questions,
`none,full`, `temperature: 0.7`, gates all pass. This is the first dispatch in the record that asked the
loader for a **corrected label set** instead of re-scoring somebody else's artefact.

| the registration said | the artefact says |
| --- | --- |
| `n` is 283, not 350 | `n.total` 283, `n.eval` 283, `qualifying` 283 |
| 67 of the slice's questions are unlabelable | 350 − 283 = 67; the revision's drop list holds 81 for all of Mini-Dev, 67 inside this slice |
| `dataset_gold` is not null | `bird-minidev-arcwise-sql-only.json`, digest `e7bf7640…e8395`, 498 entries, **129 replaced, 288 already agreed, 0 unmatched, 81 dropped** |
| baseline in 57–63% | **59.36%** (168 of 283) |
| baseline not near 51.26% | 8.1pp above it — the 8.7pp the mixture was short by |
| memory arm within 4pp | **0.00pp**: 59.36% against 59.36% |

**59.36 against 59.64 is the number that matters.** R75 re-scored fourteen artefacts with a different
instrument and predicted this population's corrected baseline at 59.64%; the dispatch measured 59.36%,
**0.28pp apart**, a tenth of the paired noise on 283 questions. Until now this lane predicted directions;
this is the first level it predicted.

**Zero delta with 283 of 283 statements differing.** The pack rewrote every answer's text and moved no
verdict: the same 168 questions are right in both arms. That is R74's reshuffle at a fifth of the
population and a fifth of the cost, and it is only visible because the artefact carries statements
rather than verdicts. A delta of exactly zero would otherwise be indistinguishable from an arm that was
never rendered.

**And the nine hundred calls were 90% cache**: 859 of 920 distillation requests came back from the
restored cache, which is the amortised shape Amendment 1 priced.

### 173.29 — The quarter of the pack that never fired is really about a sixth, and 346 draws would say which

R77's headline was that **113 of 472 rules (23.9%) never changed an answer**. The draw counts make that
number unusable as a pruning criterion: 59 of the 113 were drawn **once**, the median is three, and a
rule live on half its draws is silent on three of them 12.5% of the time.

`silenceReading` prices the silence against the rate the rules that *fired* demonstrated:

| reading | value |
| --- | --- |
| per-draw live rate of the rules that fired | **49.9%** |
| silences that rate predicts among the 113 | **38.2** |
| **excess: rules the draw counts cannot explain** | **74.8 — 15.9% of the pack, not 23.9%** |
| silent rules holding fewer than 5 draws (silence = chance < 5%) | **105 of 113** |
| extra draws that would bring every silent rule to 5 | **346** |

Rules that never fired are excluded from the rate estimate, because including them is circular — nine
rules silent on ten draws each would drag a pack-wide rate to 1/92 and then declare all nine expected.
A zero rate returns a zero target rather than a number: silence is then not a chance event at any sample
size, and a number would read as "more draws would settle it" when nothing would.

So the honest statement about R77's pack is **"about 75 rules are dead weight, and 105 of the 113 have
not been drawn enough to tell"**, and the experiment that separates them costs **346 loo draws** —
roughly a sixth of R77's evaluation bill. That is the next registration rather than a pruning.

### 173.30 — The step timeout and the lane's deadline were the same claim, and nothing compared them

R68's third attempt (`42904695578`) spent **2,961 calls over four folds and a fifth evaluation** and then
died at

```
##[error]The action 'Run the benchmark' has timed out after 200 minutes.
No files were found with the provided path: eval/results/poc-sota-bird*.partial.json
```

The dispatch was sent with `deadline_min: 300`; the step carried a literal `timeout-minutes: 200`,
chosen against the *default* deadline of 130. The lane stops itself before the runner does so that the
folds it paid for are published as a partial artefact — a dispatch that raises the deadline without
raising the timeout converts that graceful stop into a kill, and the kill discards everything.

**Structural, not remembered:**

| layer | before | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the step | literal 200 | `fromJSON(steps.deadline.outputs.timeout)` — the guard computes it |
| a dispatch | accepted any deadline | `Require a deadline the job can honour` refuses one that cannot fit 340 minutes, **before the first call** |
| the checker | four rules | five: a step that reads `SOTA_DEADLINE_MIN` may not carry a literal timeout, with a self-test reproducing this case |

The expression had to move into a shell step because GitHub's parser refuses arithmetic inside
`timeout-minutes` (`Unexpected symbol: '+'`, HTTP 422, the workflow stops parsing entirely) — a fix that
itself cost one failed dispatch to find.

**And the first correction was wrong.** The instinct was to halve the population to fit the clock. The
run's own log says a fold is ~530 calls and the whole experiment was ~3,420 calls in ~220 minutes: it was
**twenty minutes** from finishing. Halving would have paid for a thirty-minute overrun with 1.4× the
interval on the share, so the amendment withdraws it and re-dispatches at the registered 350 questions
with `max_calls` 3,700 rather than 6,300 — the cap was a forecast from a plan, and the measurement now
exists.

### 173.31 — A quarter of the pack is a sixth, and the top-up that would settle it cannot be flown

`silenceTargets` prices R77's tail as a purchase order: **105 rules, 346 draws** short of five, written
to `eval/manifests/loo/R77-silent-tail.json` and read by the lane from the registration's `looTargets`
header. `targetedLooIndex` balances those draws — least-drawn target in the pack, hash breaking ties —
and is mutation-checked both ways.

**Then the plan refuses its own dispatch.** A planned draw lands only when the question's pack contains
one of the plan's rules, and R77 measures that at **18.4%** (mean pack 1.83 rules). 346 draws therefore
need **1,875 questions and 5,625 calls — six hours**, past the job limit:

| design | pairs | calls | needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| targeted `loo` over a larger population | 346 | **5,625** | nothing new |
| force-recall `plant-r` against the pack it was added to | 346 | **692** | a new arm and its gates |

The reason is the finding: **the tail is under-drawn because the retriever rarely offers it**, and a rule
that is never recalled cannot be measured by withholding it from a pack it is not in. R78 is registered
undispatched with both designs costed; nothing is pruned on the strength of 113 silences, 105 of which
have not been drawn five times.


### 173.32 — The six hours were another backbone's, and the fix was in a different experiment's log

R78 was registered **undispatched** on the strength of one row: *wall clock at the measured 15.6
calls/minute = six hours, past the job limit*. Every other row of that table was right. The rate was not.

`15.6 calls/minute` is `zhipu:glm-4.7-flashx` — the backbone R68 dispatches. This lane runs
`deepseek-flash`, and R77's own job says what it does: 6,946 calls between 23:27:00 and 23:55:45, which
is **248 calls/minute**.

| reading | value |
| --- | --- |
| R77's model calls | 6,946 |
| R77's model window | 28.7 min |
| measured rate on `deepseek-flash` | **248 calls/min** |
| R78's projected calls (5,700 evaluation + ~3,500 learning on new questions) | **9,200** |
| wall clock at the measured rate | **37 min** |
| the job's own limit | 340 min |

**The error has a shape worth naming**: a throughput figure was carried from one experiment to another
because both were "this repository's BIRD lane". A cache key, a provider and a concurrency setting each
make that borrowing false without anybody editing a number, and the number had been used to *reject* an
experiment rather than to size one. The register now says the rate and the artefact it came from.

### 173.33 — A top-up cannot be a prefix, and nothing compared the sample with the header

`SOTA_LIMIT` could only return the first N questions. R77 scored questions 0–1,999, so "size it at 1,875"
would have scored **1,875 of the same 2,000** and re-bought every pair it already held: at temperature
zero, the same pack without the same rule is the same call, so a re-draw cannot return new information.

`offset` now exists in three places that are checked against each other:

| layer | before | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the lane | `ordered.slice(0, limit)` | `ordered.slice(offset, offset + limit)`, refusing an offset past the corpus |
| the registration | no key | `offset:` in the header, `-1` and `1.5` refused |
| the dispatch | nothing to say | resolved **from the header** by `eval:prereg-population`, so the two cannot drift |

The corpus this split can score is **7,829** questions (`[sota] selection: 7829 of 9428` in R77's log).
R78 declares `offset: 2000, n: 1900`, so it scores questions 2,000–3,899 with **zero overlap** and 3,930
still unused behind it.

**And `sample` had never been compared with anything.** It has been in every header since the first
registration; the lane read `SOTA_LIMIT` and the artefact reported whatever that was. `populationAgainstRegistration` refuses a dispatch that draws a different population from the file it claims to execute —
the same defect as R67's arm list, found in the field next to it four days later.

### 173.34 — The plan was one draw short, and a test now reads the header instead of the sentence

346 draws at the measured 18.45% hit rate need **1,876** questions. The registration said 1,875, which is
345.9, which floors to **345** — one draw short of a plan that needs 346, and the difference between a
plan fully bought and one that is not.

The test reads this file's own header and asserts `floor(sample × 369 / 2000) ≥ 346`, so the sentence can
no longer be right about its method and wrong about its arithmetic by one unit. `n = 1,900` buys 350.

### 173.35 — The excess has an interval, and its lower bound is two thirds of the estimate

R77's most-quoted number was 74.8 rules of dead weight — a point estimate whose input, the 49.9% per-draw
live rate of the rules that fired, is itself **a measured proportion**. `silenceReading` now reports the
interval, and reports it without resampling: the excess is strictly increasing in the rate, so the bounds
are the same arithmetic evaluated at the rate's own Wilson endpoints and a replay returns the same
numbers.

| reading | value | 95% |
| --- | --- | --- |
| per-draw live rate of the rules that fired | 49.9% | **47.6 – 52.2%** |
| silences that rate explains | 38.2 | — |
| **excess** | **74.8** | **72.5 – 77.1** |
| share of the 472 rules | 15.85% | **15.36 – 16.33%** |

**Dead weight exists**: the lower bound is 72.5 rules, 15.4% of the pack, and no plausible error in the
working rate closes the interval onto zero. "55.73% inert pairs might be entirely a sampling artifact" is
refuted by the file that produced it. What the interval cannot say is **which** rules, and a pruning
needs identities — which is the whole remaining job of R78, now dispatched at 2,000/1,900.

`silenceReading` calls the same `wilsonInterval` the published-cell catalogue uses rather than carrying a
second copy: two Wilson intervals in one package that disagreed in the fourth decimal would be two
numbers a reader has to reconcile, and the copied one would be the one nobody re-derived.

### 173.36 — The memory's net effect is inside ±1.4pp on every split, and that is the project's largest number

Four dispatches, three splits, two backbones, and the one quantity every improvement is supposed to move
has never been separated from zero:

| artefact | split | n | memory effect | 95% | p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `poc-sota-bird.json` (2026-10-26, `deepseek-chat`) | Mini-Dev | 350 | **−2.86pp** | −6.00 … +0.29 | 0.099 |
| `R63-recall-order` (`deepseek-flash`) | Mini-Dev | 350 | **+0.57pp** | −2.86 … +4.00 | — |
| `R77-inert-share` (`deepseek-flash`) | train, offset 0 | 2,000 | **+0.25pp** | −0.90 … +1.40 | 0.731 |
| `R68` (in flight, `zhipu:glm-4.7-flashx`) | Mini-Dev | 350 | — | — | — |

The sign moves between dispatches and the interval covers zero every time. **R77 is the informative one**:
2,000 paired questions put the effect inside **±1.4pp**, which is the tightest statement this project can
make about its own memory — tighter than any of the improvements the arm ladder has tried to
measure.

**What that reframes.** Every round of arm work has asked *which* formulation of the pack is better,
at a sample size where a 1pp difference is invisible. On the two splits measured, the whole pack moves the
verdict by less than the noise it was measured against, while occupying **1,083 characters of every
prompt** (`mean_pack_chars`, R77) and 1.83 rules of context. The dead weight R77 found — 16% of the pack,
now with an interval — is a real defect, but it is a defect *inside* a component whose total contribution
is already indistinguishable from zero. **Pruning it is not how the memory becomes useful; it is how the
memory becomes cheap.**

**The one thing R77 does separate.** `full` beats `loo` by **0.90pp** (p = 0.089, 59 lost against 41
gained): the *last* rule in a pack does more than the pack does. Adding a rule to an empty context and
adding a rule to a one-rule pack are not the same intervention, and the arithmetic says the first is worth
less than the second. That is a dose-response question this lane has never asked at the pack's actual size,
and it is the mechanism the "memory hurts" reading needs before it can be called a mechanism at all.

**Where that leaves the queue.** R78 names the 105 silent rules so a pruning can have identities; the
experiment it enables is a `full`-against-`full-pruned` pair on the same questions, which is the first
test in this project that would ask whether *removing* memory helps. On the numbers above, the honest
prior is that it does not — and that the effect to chase is not the pack's content but its size.
